items.title: Sources of banking regulation and the definition of banking
items.core_explanation_md:
Banking in India is governed mainly by the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and the **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**. The Reserve Bank and the Government control banks **from opening to winding up**.

**The provisions do not apply uniformly**: they depend on whether the bank is a **statutory corporation**, a **banking company** or a **co-operative society**.

**Definition (Section 5(b), as the courseware cites it):** *accepting, for the purpose of **lending or investing**, **deposits of money from the public**, **repayable on demand or otherwise** and **withdrawable by cheque, draft, order or otherwise**.*

So a bank does **two essential things:** **accepts deposits from the public** and **lends or invests** them. Accepting from the public does **not** mean accepting from anyone: a bank can **refuse undesirable customers**, and account opening follows **KYC norms**, with **suspicious transactions reported** under anti-money laundering rules.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A deposit-taker that does not lend or invest the deposits is not a bank under the definition.

self_check.prompt_text: What two functions make a business a bank under the definition?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Accepting deposits from the public and lending or investing them.

items.title: Deposits by cheque, licensing and the use of the word bank
items.core_explanation_md:
- **Deposits withdrawable by cheque (Section 49A):** only a **banking company**, the **Reserve Bank**, the **State Bank of India** or another body **notified by the Central Government** may accept them.
- **Non-banking financial companies** may accept public deposits but under **Reserve Bank directions** (Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act), not as banks.
- **Licence (Section 22):** a **licence from the Reserve Bank** is needed to **start or carry on banking**.
- **Name (Section 7):** a banking company **must use the word bank** in its name; **no other company, firm or individual** may use **bank, banker or banking**. **Exemptions** include subsidiaries of banks, associations of banks, **primary credit societies**, certain **co-operative societies** and the **State Bank and nationalised banks**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The licence and the name rules protect the public from unlicensed deposit-takers posing as banks.

self_check.prompt_text: Who needs a licence under Section 22 to carry on banking?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A banking company, which needs a licence from the Reserve Bank.

items.title: Permitted and prohibited business of banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Permitted (Section 6(1), examples):** dealing in **bills of exchange**; **lending and advancing money**; **guarantee and indemnity business**; **realising property** that comes into the bank's possession in satisfaction of its claims; and other business the **Central Government notifies**.

**Prohibited (Section 8):** a bank shall **not engage in trading** or **undertake trading risks**; **buying, selling or bartering goods** is prohibited. *Goods* = every kind of **moveable property** except **actionable claims, stocks, shares, money, bullion and specie** and the instruments in Section 6(1). A bank **can realise securities** taken for a loan, can **buy, sell or barter for others** in connection with **bills for collection or negotiation** and can act as **executor or trustee**.

**Non-banking assets (Section 9):** a bank **cannot hold immovable property** acquired in satisfaction of claims for **more than seven years** (except for its own use); the Reserve Bank may extend by **up to five years** if in the **depositors' interest**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The rule keeps banks from taking trading risks with depositors money.

self_check.prompt_text: For how long may a bank hold immovable property acquired in satisfaction of claims?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Not more than seven years, extendable by up to five years by the Reserve Bank.

items.title: Constitution of banks in India
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank in India is one of: a **body corporate under a special statute**; a **company** under the **Companies Act** (or a **foreign company**); or a **co-operative society** under a **Central or State enactment**.

| Type | Constituted under |
| --- | --- |
| **Public sector banks (other than SBI)** | **Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts, 1970 and 1980**: Section 3 vests the **undertakings of nationalised banks** in new statutory bodies |
| **State Bank of India** | **State Bank of India Act, 1955**; the seven associate banks (Subsidiary Banks Act, 1959) **merged with SBI**, completed in **2017-18** |
| **Regional Rural Banks** | **Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976** plus some provisions of the BR Act and RBI Act |
| **Private sector banks** (including micro and small finance banks) | **Companies Act** |
| **Foreign banks** | **Foreign companies**; certain Companies Act provisions apply; the **BR Act and RBI Act govern their banking business in India** |
| **Co-operative banks** | **Co-operative Societies Acts** (state or multi-state) |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The founding statute decides which parts of the banking laws apply.

self_check.prompt_text: Under which Act were Regional Rural Banks constituted?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976.

items.title: Co-operative banks and dual control
items.core_explanation_md:
A co-operative bank does ordinary banking on a **co-operative basis**. Structure: **urban co-operative banks** (scheduled or non-scheduled, multi-state or single-state) and **rural co-operatives**: **long term** (state and primary co-operative agriculture and rural development banks) and **short term** (**state co-operative banks**, **district central co-operative banks**, **primary agricultural credit societies**).

- **More than one state:** the **Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act**; otherwise the **State Co-operative Societies Act**.
- **Banking Laws (Application to Co-operative Societies) Act, 1965** extended parts of the BR Act and RBI Act to them (**Section 56** of the BR Act).
- **Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020** (after the **PMC Bank** failure) gave the Reserve Bank **more control** over **management, capital, audit and liquidation**, including **supersession of boards** and **restructuring**.
- Under Section 56 **references are modified**: banking company becomes **co-operative bank**; memorandum or articles become **bye-laws**; **Registrar of Companies** becomes the **Registrar of Co-operative Societies**.

**Dual control:** **State Governments and Registrars** control **formation, management and winding up**; the **Reserve Bank** controls **banking licence and regulation of banking business**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Two authorities share control, which is why co-operative bank failures needed a legal change.

self_check.prompt_text: Who controls the banking regulation of a co-operative bank and who controls its management as a society?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Reserve Bank regulates the banking business; the State Government and Registrar control its formation, management and winding up as a society.

items.title: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
items.core_explanation_md:
**Purpose:** to constitute the Reserve Bank, to **regulate the issue of bank notes**, to **keep reserves** to secure **monetary stability** and to operate the **currency and credit system** to the country's advantage.

**What the Act deals with:** the **constitution, powers and functions** of the Reserve Bank; it does **not directly regulate banks**, except **Section 42** (**cash reserves** of scheduled banks with the Reserve Bank) and **Section 18** (**direct discount of bills**).

**Central Board:** a **Governor** and not more than **four Deputy Governors**; **four directors** (one from each **local board**); **ten directors** nominated by the Government; **two government officials**.

**Scheduled bank:** a bank in the **Second Schedule** of the Act, meeting the criteria of **Section 42(6)(a)**.

**Selected sections (as cited):** **3** constitution; **4** capital; **7** management; **8** Central Board; **17** business it may transact; **19** business it may not transact; **22** issue of notes; **30** supersession of the Central Board; **42** cash reserves.

**Lender of last resort:** the Reserve Bank offers funds to institutions in difficulty (**Sections 17 and 18**). **2019 amendments** gave it powers over **non-banking financial companies**: replace or supersede boards, **remove or debar auditors**, frame **schemes of amalgamation or splitting** and direct **group company information**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: As lender of last resort the central bank can prevent one bank failure becoming a systemic crisis.

self_check.prompt_text: Which section of the RBI Act deals with the cash reserves of scheduled banks?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Section 42.

items.title: The Banking Regulation Act, 1949
items.core_explanation_md:
**Background:** passed as the **Banking Companies Act, 1949**, in force from **16 March 1949**; renamed the **Banking Regulation Act** from **1 March 1966**; **extended to co-operative banks** in **1965** by adding **Section 56**.

**Covers:** the **definition of banking**, **licensing**, **capital and reserve requirements**, **operations and management**, **liquidity**, **inspection**, and the **takeover, amalgamation and liquidation** of banks.

**Powers of the Reserve Bank:** **licence banks**, regulate **shareholding and voting rights**, supervise the **board and managers**, regulate **operations**, set **audit instructions**, order **moratorium, mergers and liquidation**, issue **directives** and **impose penalties**.

**Amendments (as the courseware describes):** **2017**: **Sections 35AA and 35AB** let the Reserve Bank direct banks to start **insolvency resolution** (under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code); **2012**: the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund** takes over **deposits inoperative for ten years**; the Reserve Bank conducts an **annual financial inspection** (**Section 35**) and **risk-based supervision**.

**Objectives:** give **specific legislation** for banking; **prevent bank failures** through **minimum capital**; ensure **balanced growth**; give the Reserve Bank **specific powers**; **safeguard depositors**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Act is the main statute for the day-to-day regulation of banking companies.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two objectives of the Banking Regulation Act.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example preventing bank failures through minimum capital, and safeguarding the interest of depositors.

items.title: The Reserve Bank and the Government as regulators
items.core_explanation_md:
**Reserve Bank powers as regulator and supervisor:** **issue licences**; **appoint and remove managerial personnel or boards**; **regulate business**; **give directions**; **inspect and supervise**; **audit**; **collect and furnish credit information**; **moratorium, amalgamation and winding up**; **impose penalties**. The **Department of Non-Banking Supervision** regulates **non-banking financial companies**.

**The Government's role:**

- It is the **sole shareholder** of the Reserve Bank and **appoints** its Governor and Central Board members.
- **Section 7(1) RBI Act:** it can give **directions in the public interest** after consulting the Governor (rarely used; first in **October 2018**, as the courseware says).
- **Appeals** lie to the Government against removal of managerial personnel (**Sections 10B and 36AA**), **cancellation of a banking licence** (**Section 22**) and refusal of a certificate on **floating charges** (**Section 14A**).
- It may **suspend or exempt** operations (**Sections 4 and 53**), **notify other banking business** (**Section 6(1)**), make **rules** (**Sections 52 and 45Y**), approve **subsidiaries** (**Section 19**), appoint a **court liquidator** (**Section 38A**) and **acquire undertakings** (**Section 36AE**).
- It holds **50 per cent or more** of the shares of **SBI, nationalised banks and RRBs** and so controls their management.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Reserve Bank is the primary regulator but the Government keeps a layer of appellate and rule-making power.

self_check.prompt_text: What share of public sector bank shares does the Central Government hold, according to the courseware?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 50 per cent or more.

items.title: Regulation of banks by other authorities
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank is also subject to **other regulators** in its other activities:

| Area | Authority |
| --- | --- |
| **Company matters** | **Companies Act** |
| **Workmen, premises, contract labour** | **Labour authorities** |
| **Taxes** | **Income tax, GST and others** |
| **Dealing in shares and debentures; public issue of capital** | **SEBI** (Securities Contract (Regulation) Act, 1956; SEBI Act, 1992) |
| **Insurance business** | **IRDAI** |
| **Mutual fund and merchant banking** | **Reserve Bank and SEBI** rules |

Under **Section 6** of the Banking Regulation Act banks may do **certain non-banking business** but in that case are **subject to the other agency's control**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A bank can be regulated by several bodies at the same time, each for a different activity.

self_check.prompt_text: Which authority regulates a bank public issue of capital?
self_check.expected_takeaway: SEBI (the Securities and Exchange Board of India).

items.title: Foreign banks, on-tap licensing and cancellation of a licence
items.core_explanation_md:
**Foreign banks** must show the Reserve Bank that they face **adequate prudential supervision at home** (with regard to **Basel standards**), that the **home regulator approves** the branch or wholly owned subsidiary, and that the home country **does not discriminate** against Indian banks. Other factors: **political and economic relations**, **financial soundness**, **ownership**, **ranking and ratings** and **international presence**.

**Licensing policy (as the courseware tells it):** new bank guidelines in **February 2013**; discussion paper on **continuous authorisation** (**August 2013**); **on tap** licensing guidelines for private sector **universal banks** on **1 August 2016**. Small finance banks: first guidelines in **2014**; on tap guidelines on **5 December 2019**. A **small finance bank** is a **public limited company** under the **Companies Act, 2013**, licensed under **Section 22** and given **scheduled bank** status once it starts operations.

**Cancellation (Section 22(4)):** the Reserve Bank may cancel if the company **stops banking in India** or **fails to meet a licence condition** (normally after giving a chance to comply). **Appeal** to the **Central Government within thirty days**; that decision is **final**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: On-tap licensing replaced the stop-and-go approach that opened applications only at intervals.

self_check.prompt_text: Within how many days of the decision may a bank appeal against cancellation of its licence?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Thirty days, to the Central Government.

items.title: Opening and shifting of branches (Section 23)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Prior Reserve Bank permission** is needed to **open a new place of business** in India or abroad, or to **change the location** of an existing one, **except within the same city, town or village**.

**No permission** is needed for a **temporary place of business** for **up to one month** in a city, town or village (or environs) where the bank already has a place, to give banking facilities at an **exhibition, conference or mela**.

Before granting permission the Reserve Bank may examine **financial condition and history**, **management**, **capital structure and earning prospects**, and whether **public interest** is served; it may attach **conditions** and **revoke** the permission after a hearing if they are broken.

**Place of business** (Section 23(5)) includes a **sub-office, pay office, sub-pay office** or any place where **deposits are received, cheques cashed or money lent**.

**Regional Rural Banks** also get their permission from the Reserve Bank, but applications are **routed through NABARD**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The same-city exemption lets a bank move a branch locally without permission, but a move to another town needs approval.

self_check.prompt_text: For how long may a bank run a temporary place of business without permission at an exhibition?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Not more than one month.

items.title: Paid-up capital, reserves and capital structure (Sections 11 and 12)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Section 11** sets **minimum paid-up capital and reserves** for a company wishing to begin banking. The amount depends on the **number of States** and **places of business** and whether **Mumbai or Kolkata** is included. The figures in the courseware are the old statutory scale; this unit teaches the **structure**, not the rupee amounts. A dispute about computing a 'place of business' is settled by the **Reserve Bank**.

**Foreign banks** must **deposit and keep with the Reserve Bank** a prescribed amount in **cash or approved securities**, and also **twenty per cent of each year's profit** from Indian branches; on cessation the deposits become **assets with a first charge for Indian creditors**.

**Section 12(1) capital structure:**

- **Subscribed capital** is **not less than half of authorised capital**.
- **Paid-up capital** is **not less than half of subscribed capital**.
- When capital is raised the test must be met **within two years** (as the Reserve Bank allows).

Banks may issue **equity shares** and **preference shares** (perpetual, irredeemable or redeemable) under **Reserve Bank guidelines**. The **Reserve Bank** has set **separate capital norms** for **small finance** and **universal banks** in its licensing policy.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The half-and-half tests stop a bank advertising a large authorised capital while collecting little from shareholders.

self_check.prompt_text: What fraction of subscribed capital must be paid up under Section 12(1)?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At least one-half.

items.title: Shareholding, voting rights, commission and dividend
items.core_explanation_md:
- **Voting cap (Section 12(2)):** no shareholder may vote more than **10 per cent** of total voting rights; the Reserve Bank may **raise the cap in phases to 26 per cent**.
- **Prior approval (Section 12B):** anyone who would hold **5 per cent or more** of **paid-up capital or voting rights** needs **Reserve Bank approval**; a bank that gets a transfer request taking a party over **5 per cent** must refer it. The goal: control stays with **fit and proper** persons.
- **Section 12(3):** a registered shareholder cannot be sued on the ground that title to the shares is with another, except by a **transferee** or on behalf of a **minor or lunatic**.
- **Reports:** shareholding of the **Chairman, MD or CEO** is reported to the Reserve Bank.
- **Section 13:** commission, brokerage or discount on the sale of bank shares is capped at **2.5 per cent of the issue price**.
- **Section 15:** **no dividend** until all **capitalised expenses** are written off; **Section 17:** a specified part of profit goes to the **statutory reserve fund**.

The courseware also states Reserve Bank **conditions on dividends** (current-year profit, capital adequacy and net NPA tests); these are **not taught here** because later directions replaced them.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 5 per cent approval limit and the 10 per cent voting cap work together: the first screens who enters, the second limits their say.

self_check.prompt_text: What share of paid-up capital or voting rights needs prior Reserve Bank approval to acquire?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Five per cent or more.

items.title: Subsidiaries and shareholding in other companies (Sections 19 and 29A)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Section 19** stops banks from running **trading activities** through **controlling interests in non-banking companies**.

**A bank may form a subsidiary only to:**

1. do any **Section 6(1) business** (clauses (a) to (o));
2. carry on **banking exclusively outside India** (with the Reserve Bank's **prior permission**);
3. do **any other business** the Reserve Bank, with **prior Central Government approval**, finds **conducive to the spread of banking** or in the **public interest**.

Business done by a subsidiary is **not** the bank doing it for **Section 8** purposes.

**Section 19(2):** a bank may not hold shares (as **pledgee, mortgagee or absolute owner**) above **30 per cent of the company's paid-up capital** or **30 per cent of its own paid-up capital and reserves**, **whichever is less**. It may not hold shares in a company in which its **managing director or manager is interested**, except a **subsidiary**.

**Section 29A:** the Reserve Bank can order **inspection of associate enterprises** (holding or subsidiary companies, joint ventures, companies with control over the board or significant influence).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 30 per cent ceiling prevents a bank from using pledged or purchased shares to take control of trading companies.

self_check.prompt_text: Under Section 19(2), the 30 per cent share-holding ceiling applies on whichever of two measures is what?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Whichever is less: 30 per cent of the company paid-up capital or 30 per cent of the bank paid-up capital and reserves.

items.title: Board of directors (Section 10A)
items.core_explanation_md:
- **At least 51 per cent** of directors must have **special knowledge or practical experience** in **accountancy, agriculture and rural economy, banking, co-operation, economics, finance, law, small scale industry** or another useful field.
- **At least two directors** must have knowledge of **agriculture and rural economy, co-operation or small scale industry**.
- **Substantial interest:** a director must not have **substantial interest** in a company or firm in **trade, commerce or industry** as an **employee, manager or managing agent**. **Section 25 (now Section 8) companies** and **small scale industrial concerns** are excluded; **proprietors of other trading, commercial or industrial concerns** are disqualified. Substantial interest (Section 5(ne)) is a **beneficial holding above a fixed sum or ten per cent of paid-up capital**, and **above ten per cent of capital in a firm**.
- **Term:** directors other than the chairman and whole-time directors may serve **not more than eight years continuously** (courseware, to be checked after the 2025 amendments).
- **Reconstitution:** the Reserve Bank can order it, with **retirement by lots**; if the bank does not comply in **two months** the Reserve Bank may **remove a director and appoint another**. Proceedings are **not invalid** merely because of a **defect in board composition**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 51 per cent rule makes the board a mix of banking and sector expertise rather than only representatives of owners.

self_check.prompt_text: What minimum share of directors must have special knowledge or practical experience?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Fifty-one per cent.

items.title: Chairman and managing director (Sections 10B, 10BB and 10C)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Appointment:** every banking company has a **whole-time or part-time chairman** chosen from its directors; a **whole-time chairman manages the whole affairs**; a **part-time chairman needs prior Reserve Bank approval**. Without a chairman, a **managing director** runs the bank under the **board's control**. **Term:** not more than **five years**, with **re-election** possible; the holder may stay until a successor takes over, with **Reserve Bank approval**.

**Qualifications (Section 10B(4)):** special knowledge of the **working of a bank, SBI, a subsidiary bank or a financial institution**, or of **financial, economic or business administration**. **Disqualifications:** director of another company (other than a subsidiary or Section 25 company), **partner in a trading firm**, **substantial interest** elsewhere, or **engaged in any other business or vocation**.

**Removal:** if the Reserve Bank thinks the person **not fit and proper** it can require the bank to remove and replace, after a **hearing**; if the bank does not act in **two months** the Reserve Bank may remove and appoint. **Appeal** to the **Central Government within thirty days**; the decision is **final**.

**Vacancy:** temporary arrangement for **up to four months** (with Reserve Bank approval); the Reserve Bank may **appoint a chairman for up to three years** (**Section 10BB**), reappointable once. **Section 10C** exempts the chairman or MD from **qualification shares**.

Sections **10A, 10B and 10BB override other laws and contracts** and give **no right to compensation** for loss of office. The **Financial Services Institutions Bureau** (from **1 July 2022**) recommends whole-time directors and non-executive chairpersons, replacing the **Banks Board Bureau**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Reserve Bank can step in at every stage, from the qualification of the chairman to removal and filling a vacancy.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the maximum term of a whole-time chairman or managing director in one appointment?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Five years.

items.title: Additional directors, employment limits and the power to remove management
items.core_explanation_md:
**Additional directors (Section 36AB):** the Reserve Bank may appoint them **in the interest of banking policy or the public interest or of the bank and its depositors**; they serve **at the Reserve Bank's pleasure** for up to **three years** (and further periods of up to three years), are **not liable for good faith acts**, need **no qualification shares**, and are **not counted** in working out the required proportions of directors.

**Restrictions on employment (Section 10):** a bank must not employ or continue a **managing agent or employee** who is **insolvent** (or suspended payment or compounded with creditors), was **convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude**, is paid by **commission or share of profits**, or is paid **excessive** remuneration in the Reserve Bank's opinion. Commission to **brokers and agents outside the regular staff**, and **bonus under a settlement**, are not affected.

**Removal (Section 36AA):** the Reserve Bank may remove **any chairman, director, chief executive officer or other officer or employee** in the **public interest**, to stop affairs being run **detrimentally to depositors**, or to secure **proper management**.

- The person gets a **reasonable chance to represent**; in **urgent** cases the Reserve Bank may **bar the person pending** a decision.
- **Appeal** to the **Central Government within thirty days**; its decision is **final**.
- The removed person may **not take part in management for up to five years**; breach is punishable with a **fine of Rs 250 for each day**.
- A **suitable replacement** may be appointed for up to **three years**, extendable by further periods of **up to three years**.

**Supersession (Section 36ACA):** the Reserve Bank can **supersede the board for six months**, extendable up to **twelve months**, with an **Administrator** assisted by a **committee of three or more persons**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Supersession is the last step in the ladder, after director removal and additional directors fail to fix the bank.

self_check.prompt_text: For how long may the Reserve Bank first supersede a bank board under Section 36ACA?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Six months, extendable to a maximum of twelve months.

items.title: The power of the Reserve Bank to issue directions
items.core_explanation_md:
**Sections 21 and 35A** let the Reserve Bank give **directions to banks**. Directions are **binding on the banks addressed** even if not labelled statutory.

- **Section 21**: regulation of **advances**; **Section 35A**: **wide general powers**, including directions on deposit interest and lending.
- **2017 amendment**: **Sections 35AA and 35AB** let the Reserve Bank direct action on **bad loans**.
- **Case law (as the courseware cites it):** a **Master Circular under statutory power has the force of law**; a **non-statutory circular creates no legal rights**; directions bind **banks, not customers or the public**; they apply **prospectively** and do not void **contracts with third parties**; the power must be used in **good faith**.
- **Section 36(1)(a)**: the Reserve Bank may **caution or prohibit** banks against particular transactions and **give advice**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Directions are a quicker regulatory tool than amending the Act, but only those backed by statutory power carry the force of law.

self_check.prompt_text: Which sections give the Reserve Bank the power to issue binding directions to banks?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act.

items.title: Acceptance of deposits and unclaimed deposits
items.core_explanation_md:
**Types:** **time deposits** (fixed, recurring) are repayable after the agreed period; **demand deposits** (current, savings) on demand, under the agreed terms and **Reserve Bank directions**.

**Directions under Section 35A(c)** can cover **moratoria**, **minimum and maximum periods**, **NRI deposit rates**, bulk deposit and **KYC** matters.

**Deposit insurance:** under the **DICGC Act (as amended in 2021)** the account holder is paid up to the insured amount within **90 days** of a bank moratorium (the amount is not taught here as it is dated).

**Unclaimed deposits:**

- **Section 26:** annual **return within 30 days of the end of the calendar year** of all deposits **not operated for ten years** (for fixed deposits, ten years from the **expiry of the deposit period**).
- **Section 26A (2013):** deposits unclaimed for **ten years or more** pass to the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund** within **three months**; the depositor, legal heirs or nominee **can claim them back at any time**.
- **Eligible accounts:** savings, fixed or term, recurring, current, cash credit credit balances, and balances of **drafts, pay orders and bankers cheques**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Fund keeps unclaimed money usable by the depositor while the bank no longer treats it as its own liability.

self_check.prompt_text: After how many years of inactivity is a deposit transferred to the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Ten years or more.

items.title: Nomination for deposits, safe custody and lockers
items.core_explanation_md:
**Deposits (Section 45ZA):** a depositor may **nominate one person** to receive the deposit on the **death of the sole depositor or all depositors**; the nomination can be **varied or cancelled** at any time. For a **minor nominee**, a person may be **appointed to receive the money** on the minor's behalf.

**Effect:** payment to the nominee gives the bank a **valid discharge**, but a **legal heir's rights against the nominee remain** (the courts treat the nominee as holding for the heirs).

**Rules:** the **Banking Companies (Nomination) Rules, 1985** and **Co-operative Banks (Nomination) Rules, 1985**.

**Safe custody and lockers (Sections 45ZC and 45ZE):** one person may be nominated to receive the **articles** or **locker contents** after the hirer's death, after an **inventory**. Before access the bank must **verify identity and death**, **check for court orders** restraining access, and **tell the survivor or nominee** that access is **as trustee for the legal heirs**. Joint lockers follow the **survivorship clause** (either or survivor, anyone or survivor).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Nomination is a quick way to pay the bank safely, not a way to override succession law.

self_check.prompt_text: Does payment to a nominee defeat the claims of the legal heirs of the deceased depositor?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. The bank gets a valid discharge but the legal heirs may still claim against the nominee.

items.title: Interest rate regulation, MCLR and external benchmark lending
items.core_explanation_md:
**Power:** Section **21 read with Section 35A**; the Reserve Bank must **not discriminate** among classes of depositors or borrowers without legal justification.

**Deregulation:** deposit rates were not regulated until **1964**; both **deposit and lending rates are now largely free** (with exceptions for **weaker sections, exporters and small loans**).

**Benchmarks:** **BPLR (2003)** gave way to the **Base Rate (1 July 2010)**, then **MCLR (1 April 2016)**: **marginal cost of funds + negative carry on CRR + operating costs + tenor premium**. MCLR reflects the **current marginal cost**, while the Base Rate reflected the **average cost**.

**External benchmark (the courseware's 2019-20 rule):** new **floating rate retail and MSE loans** are linked to the **repo rate**, the **3-month or 6-month Treasury Bill yield** published by FBIL, or another published benchmark; **banks choose the spread**; the **credit risk premium** may change only on **substantial change in credit assessment**; the rate is **reset at least once every three months**; **one benchmark per loan category** in a bank.

**Section 21A:** a court cannot **reopen a bank transaction because the rate is excessive**; it overrides the **Usurious Loans Act, 1918**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Linking loan rates to an external benchmark makes policy rate changes pass through to borrowers faster.

self_check.prompt_text: How often must the interest rate under an external benchmark be reset at the latest?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At least once in three months.

items.title: Internet banking guidelines
items.core_explanation_md:
The Reserve Bank's Working Group looked at **technology and security**, **legal** and **regulatory and supervisory** aspects.

- **Technology:** a **Board-approved security policy**, **logical access controls** (user ids, passwords, smart cards, biometrics), **public key infrastructure** as the favoured technology, **periodic penetration tests**, **physical access controls**, **tested backups** and **disaster recovery sites**.
- **Legal:** accounts opened over the internet only after **physical verification of identity**; the **Consumer Protection Act** applies to banking services.
- **Regulatory:** **prior Reserve Bank approval** to offer internet banking; **report breaches**; only **members of the cheque clearing system** take part in inter-bank payment gateways.

The courseware also mentions the **2015 circular** for co-operative banks (**view-only** and **transactional** facilities).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Security rules matter more here than in branch banking because the customer is not physically present.

self_check.prompt_text: Whose prior approval does a bank need to provide internet banking?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Reserve Bank of India.

items.title: Regulation of money market instruments
items.core_explanation_md:
**Section 45W** (RBI Act, **Amendment Act 2006**) lets the Reserve Bank regulate **interest rate products** and **money market instruments, foreign exchange and derivatives** in public interest; it does **not** extend to **trades on recognised stock exchanges**.

- **Call, notice and term money:** participants include **scheduled commercial banks, payment banks, small finance banks, RRBs, co-operative banks and primary dealers**; **prudential borrowing limits** apply (dated figures not taught).
- **Certificates of deposit:** issued by **scheduled commercial banks, RRBs and small finance banks** in **dematerialised form**; **no loans against CDs**.
- **Commercial paper:** a **money market instrument** under **Section 45W**; issued as a **promissory note at a discount**, in **dematerialised form**, **minimum rating A3**, **no underwriting or co-acceptance**, **no call or put options**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: These instruments are short term and mostly wholesale, which is why the Reserve Bank directs rather than legislates for them.

self_check.prompt_text: Under which section is commercial paper treated as a money market instrument regulated by the Reserve Bank?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Section 45W of the Reserve Bank of India Act.

items.title: The Banking Ombudsman and the Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021
items.core_explanation_md:
An **Ombudsman** is an **independent, non-partisan** authority that handles public grievances as an **alternative to court**.

**History:** **Banking Ombudsman Scheme 1995** under **Section 35A** (modified 2002; **2006 Scheme**). The **Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021** merged the **Banking Ombudsman Scheme 2006**, the **Ombudsman Scheme for NBFCs 2018** and the **Ombudsman Scheme for Digital Transactions 2019**, which were **repealed**.

**Integrated Scheme features:** complaint if the entity **did not reply within 30 days** or the customer is **dissatisfied**; **deficiency in service** is the ground, with listed **exclusions**; the complainant need **not name the scheme**; **no territorial jurisdiction per office**; a **Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre at Chandigarh**; the regulated entity appoints a **Principal Nodal Officer** not below **General Manager rank**; an entity **cannot appeal** if it did not give **timely information**; the **Executive Director in charge of Consumer Education and Protection Department** is the **Appellate Authority**.

The ombudsman **follows Reserve Bank directions** and does **not proceed** on a matter taken to **court, tribunal or arbitration**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Merging three schemes meant a customer no longer needed to know which scheme covered the regulated entity.

self_check.prompt_text: Within how many days of the entity not replying may a customer approach the ombudsman under the Integrated Scheme?
self_check.expected_takeaway: After thirty days with no reply or an unsatisfactory reply.

items.title: Financial stability and the reserve fund (Section 17)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Financial stability** (Reserve Bank): a situation where the financial sector provides **critical services to the real economy without discontinuity**.

**Provisions that promote it:** the **reserve fund**, **cash reserve**, **statutory liquidity ratio** and **assets in India**.

**Reserve fund (Section 17(1)):** every banking company incorporated in India transfers **not less than 20 per cent of its profit** (per the profit and loss account) to the reserve fund **before declaring any dividend**. The courseware adds that the **Reserve Bank instructed 25 per cent** of net profit after tax for commercial banks (other than foreign banks) from the year ended **31 March 2001** (flagged as unverified).

- **Exemption:** the Government may exempt on the Reserve Bank's recommendation if capital and reserves are adequate against deposits, but not unless the **reserve fund plus share premium account is at least the paid-up capital**.
- **Appropriation** from the fund must be **reported within 21 days**.
- **Foreign banks** do not create the fund; they **deposit 20 per cent of annual Indian profit** with the Reserve Bank (**Section 11(2)**).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Retained reserves build a cushion that lets the bank absorb losses before they hit depositors.

self_check.prompt_text: What minimum share of profit must a banking company transfer to the reserve fund under Section 17(1)?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Twenty per cent.

items.title: Cash reserve (CRR) under Section 42 of the RBI Act
items.core_explanation_md:
**Who:** every **scheduled bank** keeps a cash reserve with the Reserve Bank (**Section 42**); **non-scheduled banks** under **Section 18 of the BR Act**.

**Scheduled bank (Second Schedule):** the Reserve Bank may include a bank that has **paid-up capital and reserves of at least Rs 5 lakh**, whose affairs are **not detrimental to depositors**, and that is a **State co-operative bank, a company, a notified institution or a foreign company**; it may **exclude** a bank that falls below Rs 5 lakh, is run detrimentally or goes into **liquidation**.

**Quantum (Section 42(1), 2006 amendment):** an **average daily balance** of a **percentage of demand and time liabilities in India** notified by the Reserve Bank, with **no floor or ceiling** in the Act. **No interest** is paid on CRR balances. The courseware states that a **minimum of 90 per cent** of the required balance must be kept **every day** of the fortnight.

**Returns:** a **signed return by two officers**, within **seven days** of every **alternate Friday**.

**Penalty:** **3 per cent above the bank rate** on the shortfall in the **first fortnight** and **5 per cent above** if it **continues**; further default makes **directors, managers or secretaries** liable to a **fine**; the Reserve Bank may **bar fresh deposits**; the penalty is due within **14 days** of demand.

**Non-scheduled banks:** at least **3 per cent** of demand and time liabilities, in cash or a **current account with the Reserve Bank**, with a **monthly return** by the **20th**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The CRR gives the Reserve Bank a lever over money supply and a guaranteed pool of liquidity held at the central bank.

self_check.prompt_text: What penal rate applies to a first-fortnight CRR shortfall?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Three per cent above the bank rate.

items.title: Statutory liquidity ratio and assets in India
items.core_explanation_md:
**SLR (Section 24 of the BR Act):** every bank holds a **percentage of net demand and time liabilities** as **liquid assets in India**, in the form notified by the Reserve Bank. After the **2007 Ordinance** the Act has **no 25 per cent floor**; the Reserve Bank can set the ratio **up to 40 per cent** of net demand and time liabilities. **Non-scheduled banks** hold SLR assets **in addition to their Section 18 cash reserve**.

**Returns:** a **monthly return within 20 days** of the month end, with positions on **every alternate Friday**.

**Penalty:** **3 per cent above the bank rate** on a shortfall, rising to **5 per cent above** if it continues; **directors, managers and secretaries** are liable to a **fine** on continued default; the Reserve Bank may **waive** it where there was **sufficient reason**.

**Assets in India (Section 25):** on the **last Friday of every quarter**, assets in India must be at least **75 per cent of demand and time liabilities in India**; the return is due **within a month of the quarter end** (RRBs report to **NABARD**). Assets include **cash, gold, unencumbered approved securities** and approved **export and import bills**; **paid-up capital, reserves and credit balance in the profit and loss account** are **not liabilities in India**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: SLR and the assets in India rule together keep banking funds invested in safe, liquid assets inside the country.

self_check.prompt_text: What share of demand and time liabilities in India must be held as assets in India?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At least 75 per cent, at the close of the last Friday of every quarter.

items.title: Annual accounts and the balance sheet (Section 29)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Preparation (Section 29):** every banking company prepares its **balance sheet and profit and loss account** at the **end of each calendar year**, or at the end of **twelve months ending on another date the Central Government notifies**. **Foreign banks** cover business through **all branches in India**. Banks follow **Reserve Bank directions** on **income recognition, asset classification and provisioning**.

**Signature:** by the **manager or principal officer** and **at least three directors** (all directors if there are three or fewer); for a foreign bank, by the **manager or agent** at the principal office in India.

**Form:** the **Third Schedule**, which the Government may amend after **three months' notice**. The **Banking Regulation Act overrides** the Companies Act on the form and the true-and-fair-view requirement.

**Publication (Section 31):** with the auditor's report, in a **newspaper circulating at the place of the principal office**, **within six months** of the period end.

**To the Reserve Bank:** **three copies within three months** of the period end, **extendable by a further three months**. **To the Registrar of Companies:** **three copies** (Section 32).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Act gives banks their own accounting framework because the Reserve Bank needs the accounts in a uniform form.

self_check.prompt_text: Within how many months of the end of the period must a bank submit three copies of its accounts to the Reserve Bank?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Within three months, extendable by a further three months.

items.title: Audit and auditors (Section 30) and special audit
items.core_explanation_md:
**Audit (Section 30(1)):** by a person **qualified to be a company auditor**. **Section 30(1A):** **Reserve Bank approval** is needed to **appoint, re-appoint or remove** the auditor.

**Duties:** the auditor has the **Companies Act** powers and liabilities and reports on the **adequacy of information and explanations**, whether transactions are **within the company's powers**, whether **branch returns** were adequate, whether the **profit and loss account is true**, and any matter for the **shareholders' attention**.

**Wider responsibility:** the auditor owes duties to **depositors and the public** because the bank deals in **public money**. The **2018 Enforcement Action Framework** deals with lapses by statutory auditors of commercial banks.

**Special audit (Section 30(1B)):** the Reserve Bank may order it **in the public interest** or in the interest of the **bank or its depositors**, for any **transaction, class of transactions or period**; the auditor may be **a different qualified auditor appointed by the Reserve Bank** or the **statutory auditor**; the order **binds the bank and the auditor**; the **report goes to the Reserve Bank** with a copy to the bank; the **bank pays**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A special audit gives the regulator an independent look at a specific problem without waiting for the annual audit.

self_check.prompt_text: Who bears the expenses of a special audit ordered by the Reserve Bank under Section 30(1B)?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The banking company.

items.title: Returns to the Reserve Bank
items.core_explanation_md:
| Return | Provision | Timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Liquid assets** | **Section 24(3)** (Rule 13A) | **Within 20 days** of the month end, with positions on each **alternate Friday** |
| **Monthly return of assets and liabilities** | **Section 27** (Rule 14A) | **Before the close of the next month**, showing the **last Friday** position |
| **Assets in India** | **Section 25(1)** (Rule 14A) | **Within one month** of the **quarter end** |
| **Unclaimed deposits** | **Section 26** (Rule 14B) | **Within 30 days** of the **calendar year end** |
| **Accounts and balance sheet** | **Section 29** | **Within three months**, extendable by **three more** |
| **Non-scheduled banks: cash reserve** | **Section 18** (Rule 13A) | **By the 20th of the month** |
| **Scheduled banks** | **Section 42, RBI Act** (**Form I**) | Alternate Fridays |

The Reserve Bank may also call for **any statement or information** at any time, **returns for each day** of a month, and **half-yearly** returns on **investments** and **advances by sector**.

**Penalty for a cash reserve default:** **3 per cent above the bank rate** on the shortfall and **5 per cent above** if it continues.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Returns give the regulator a regular view of liquidity and asset positions across the banking system.

items.title: Preservation of records and return of paid instruments
items.core_explanation_md:
**Section 45Y:** the Central Government, after consulting the Reserve Bank, makes **rules on how long a bank keeps its books, accounts, documents and paid instruments**. The rules are the **Banking Companies (Period of Preservation of Records) Rules, 1985** and the **Co-operative Banks** equivalent; the Reserve Bank may direct **longer periods** under **Section 35A**.

**Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005:** a bank keeps a record of all **cash transactions above Rs 10 lakh**; **connected cash transactions** below Rs 10 lakh whose **monthly total exceeds Rs 10 lakh**; **non-profit organisation receipts above Rs 10 lakh**; transactions with **forged or counterfeit notes**; and all **suspicious transactions**. The record must allow **reconstruction of a transaction**: **nature, amount and currency, date and parties**. Transaction records are kept for **at least five years** from the transaction, and **identification documents for at least five years** after the relationship ends.

**Return of paid instruments (Section 45Z):** a bank may **return a paid instrument** to the customer before the preservation period ends, but only after **making and keeping a true copy** (mechanical or other process); it may **recover the copying cost**. **Customer** includes a **Government department** and a **statutory corporation**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A true copy lets the bank return the original to the customer without losing the evidence of the transaction.

self_check.prompt_text: For how long must a bank keep records of transactions under the PML Maintenance of Records Rules as the courseware states them?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At least five years from the date of the transaction.

items.title: Inspection and scrutiny (Section 35)
items.core_explanation_md:
- **Inspection (Section 35(1)):** the Reserve Bank may inspect a bank **at any time**; the **Annual Financial Inspection** is now mainly a **risk based supervision** exercise (**SPARC**) producing a **Risk Assessment Report**. A **copy of the inspection report goes to the bank**.
- **Duties during inspection:** directors and officials must **produce all books, accounts and documents**; the inspecting officer may **examine any director or officer on oath**.
- **Inspection on Government direction:** the Reserve Bank **must inspect** and give the Government a copy; the Government may, after the bank has had an **opportunity to represent**, **prohibit fresh deposits**, **cancel or modify** an order subject to terms, and **publish** the report.
- **Scrutiny (Section 35(1A)):** by **officers at any time**; a **copy of the scrutiny report is not mandatory**, but must be given **if the bank asks** or if **adverse action** against the bank is contemplated.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Scrutiny is the lighter, quicker tool; inspection is the full examination with a report the bank must receive.

self_check.prompt_text: Is the Reserve Bank bound to give the bank a copy of a scrutiny report in all cases?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; it must give a copy if the bank asks for it or if adverse action is contemplated.

items.title: The Board for Financial Supervision
items.core_explanation_md:
**Origin:** the **Department of Banking Supervision** (1993) and the **Board for Financial Supervision (BFS)** in **November 1994**, under the **Reserve Bank of India (Board for Financial Supervision) Regulations, 1994**; **supervision of non-banking finance companies** moved to a separate department in **1997**; a **unified Department of Supervision** from **1 November 2019**.

**Composition:** the **Governor** (chairman); **one Deputy Governor**, usually the one in charge of supervision (vice chairman); **four directors of the Central Board** nominated by the Governor.

**Sub-committee (April 2018):** chaired by the **Deputy Governor in charge of supervision**; handles **payments banks, small finance banks, local area banks, small foreign banks, select urban co-operative banks and select NBFCs and credit information companies**.

**Functions:** **off-site surveillance**, **supervisory rating**, **Prompt Corrective Action** for weak banks, **fraud risk management**, **risk based supervision**, an **enforcement framework**, a **credit registry for large borrowers**, and strengthening **audit and internal controls**.

**Meetings:** normally **monthly**; **three members** (including the chairman or vice chairman) form the **quorum**. **DAKSH** (6 October 2022) is a web-based **compliance monitoring workflow**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The BFS joins bank and non-bank supervision under one authority within the Reserve Bank.

self_check.prompt_text: Who chairs the Board for Financial Supervision?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Governor of the Reserve Bank of India.

items.title: Acquisition of the undertaking of a banking company
items.core_explanation_md:
**Section 36AE:** the Central Government may **acquire the undertaking** (the **entire organisation**) of a banking company after a **Reserve Bank report**, if the bank:

- has **more than once failed to comply with written directions** under **Section 21 or 35A** on **banking policy**; or
- is **managed detrimentally** to **depositors**, **banking policy** or the **better provision of credit**.

The Government acts **after consulting the Reserve Bank**, by a **notified order** from an **appointed day**, after giving the bank a **reasonable opportunity to show cause**.

**Effect:** all **assets and liabilities vest in the Central Government**, which may vest them in a **company or corporation** (the **transferee bank**).

**Section 36AF:** a **scheme** (property, assets, liabilities, board, employees, **compensation to shareholders**) made **with the Reserve Bank**, laid before **Parliament**, with **overriding effect**.

**Section 36AG:** shareholders get **compensation** under the **Fifth Schedule**; **Section 36AH:** a **tribunal reference** is available if the offer is not acceptable.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Acquisition is the strongest step short of winding up, used when a bank defies policy directions or is badly managed.

items.title: Amalgamation, moratorium and schemes of reconstruction
items.core_explanation_md:
**Voluntary amalgamation (Section 44A):** the scheme goes to the **shareholders of both banks**; it needs a **majority in number representing two-thirds in value** of shareholders **present in person or by proxy**; a **dissenting shareholder** who gives notice may claim **the value of his shares**; the scheme then needs **Reserve Bank sanction**.

**Amalgamation by Government:** under **Section 396 of the Companies Act 1956 (Section 237 of the 2013 Act)**, **after consulting the Reserve Bank**.

**Moratorium (Section 45):** on the Reserve Bank's application the **Central Government** may stay actions and proceedings against a bank for a **fixed period, extendable, total not more than six months**; during it the bank **makes no payments to depositors** unless the Government directs.

**Scheme of reconstruction or amalgamation:** the Reserve Bank may prepare it **during or after** the moratorium **in public interest, depositors' interest, for proper management or for the banking system**. It may deal with **capital, assets and liabilities, board, memorandum, reduction of rights of members, depositors and creditors, payment and employees**. **Employees continue** on the same terms (with an **option to leave within three years**).

**Sanction and effect:** the **Central Government sanctions** the scheme after **suggestions and objections** from the banks concerned; the sanction is **conclusive evidence** of compliance; the scheme has **overriding effect**; **exemptions** can last **up to seven years**; **one scheme** can cover **several banks** under moratorium.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A moratorium buys time while the Reserve Bank designs a rescue by reconstruction or merger.

self_check.prompt_text: What shareholder majority is needed for a voluntary amalgamation under Section 44A?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A majority in number representing two-thirds in value of those present in person or by proxy, in each company.

items.title: Winding up of banking companies
items.core_explanation_md:
**Suspension (Section 37):** a bank temporarily unable to pay may apply to the **High Court** to stay proceedings for a **fixed period, total not more than six months**, supported by a **Reserve Bank report** that it will be able to pay.

**Winding up by the High Court (Section 38):** **mandatory** if the bank is **unable to pay its debts** or the **Reserve Bank applies**. The Reserve Bank **must apply** if the **Central Government directs** (Section 35(4)). It **may apply** if the bank **fails Section 11 capital requirements**, **loses its licence**, is **barred from taking deposits**, a **compromise cannot work**, the **returns show it cannot pay**, or its **continuance prejudices depositors**.

**Deemed inability to pay:** a refused **lawful demand** plus a **Reserve Bank certificate**; the time limit is **two days** where the Reserve Bank has an office or branch, **otherwise five days**. The courts leave the decision to wind up to the Reserve Bank (**Palai Central Bank**).

**Liquidators:** a **court liquidator** attached to each High Court (**Section 38A**); the Reserve Bank, State Bank or another notified bank may be **official liquidator (Section 39)**. The liquidator reports within **two months** and invites claims within **15 days**.

**Depositors:** claims are **deemed filed** from the bank's books (**Section 43**); **preferential payment** to savings depositors up to a limit (**Section 43A**), not covered by deposit insurance.

**Voluntary winding up (Section 44):** only if the **Reserve Bank certifies** the bank can **pay all debts in full**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The winding up rules favour speed and depositor protection, and let the Reserve Bank, not creditors, trigger the process.

self_check.prompt_text: For how long can a High Court stay proceedings against a bank under Section 37 at most?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Six months in total.

items.title: Penalties for contravention
items.core_explanation_md:
**RBI Act, Chapter V:** **false statements** in an application, return or statement (or wilful omission of a material fact) carry **imprisonment up to three years and a fine**; **failure to produce documents** carries a **fine**, with a **daily fine** for continuing offences. **Sections 58B(3) to 58B(5B)** cover contraventions of the **Chapter IIIB** directions.

**Companies:** **every person in charge and responsible** for the conduct of business is **deemed guilty** unless he shows the offence occurred **without his knowledge** or that he used **due diligence**. A court takes cognisance only on a **complaint by an authorised Reserve Bank officer** (except **Chapter IIIC deposit offences**); a **metropolitan magistrate or first class judicial magistrate** tries them.

**Banking Regulation Act:** **Section 46** penalises **false statements**, **failure to produce information**, **taking deposits against an order under Section 35(4)(a)** (a **fine up to twice the deposits taken**) and **other contraventions** with **fines and daily fines**. **Section 47:** cognisance only on a complaint by the Reserve Bank (or **NABARD** in some cases). **Section 47A:** the Reserve Bank may **impose a penalty itself**; if it does, **no complaint is filed in court** for the same default.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Reserve Bank can either prosecute through the courts or impose a penalty itself, but not both for the same default.

self_check.prompt_text: May a court take cognisance of a Banking Regulation Act offence on a private complaint?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; only on a complaint by an authorised Reserve Bank officer (or NABARD in some cases).

items.core_explanation_md:
**Constitution:** a **body corporate** set up under **Section 3 of the State Bank of India Act, 1955** to take over the **Imperial Bank**; **perpetual succession**, a **common seal**, can **sue and be sued**.

**Ownership:** the **Government of India holds the majority**; **no other shareholder** may exercise **voting rights above 10 per cent** unless the Central Government specifies otherwise after consulting the Reserve Bank.

**Management:** the **Central Board** has **general superintendence and direction**, acting on **business principles** with regard to **public interest**. The **Central Government** may direct the bank on **public interest policy** after consulting the **Governor** and the **Chairman**, through the Central Board. **Regulations** are made by the Board **after consulting the Reserve Bank** and with the **Central Government's prior sanction**.

**Board:** a **Chairman**, **up to four Managing Directors** appointed by the Government, plus directors for **workmen and officers**, directors nominated for **co-operative and rural economy** knowledge, and directors **elected by shareholders other than the Reserve Bank**. Chairman and MDs serve **up to five years** (re-appointable) and can be removed on **three months' notice or pay**. **Local boards** sit at each local head office (**Section 21B**).

**Business:** acts as the **agent of the Reserve Bank** at places where it has a branch and the Reserve Bank does not; may carry on **Section 5(b)** banking and **Section 6(1)** business and **acquire other banks** with Government sanction.

**Accounts and audit:** books closed on **31 March**; accounts, auditor's report and the **Central Board's report** go to the Government and the Reserve Bank **within three months**; auditor is **qualified under the Companies Act**, appointed by the **Reserve Bank with Government approval**; reports are **laid before Parliament**; shareholder particulars go **within two months**; **AGM within six weeks** of sending the balance sheet.

**Subsidiaries:** the **five associate banks and Bharatiya Mahila Bank** merged with SBI from **1 April 2017**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: SBI is the only public sector bank under its own Act, with a board structure that differs from the nationalised banks.

self_check.prompt_text: Under which Act and section was the State Bank of India established?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Section 3 of the State Bank of India Act, 1955.

items.title: Regional Rural Banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Origin:** the **Regional Rural Banks Ordinance, 1975**, replaced by the **Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976**, to serve **rural credit needs** of **small and marginal farmers, agricultural labourers, artisans and small entrepreneurs**.

**Establishment (Section 3):** by **Central Government notification** at the request of a **sponsor bank**, for **specified local limits**. **Capital (as the courseware states):** **Central Government 50 per cent**, **sponsor bank 35 per cent**, **State Government 15 per cent**.

**Character:** a **body corporate** with perpetual succession; a **compact area** of a few districts with **similar agro-climatic and rural conditions**; accepts **all types of deposits**.

**Management:** the **board** works on **business principles with due regard to public interest**; the **Central Government may direct** on public interest policy. The **chairman** is a **whole-time** officer appointed by the **sponsor bank** in **consultation with NABARD** (or by the Central Government) and **removable** by the sponsor bank. A director who is **adjudged insolvent** or **convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude** is **disqualified**; **absence from three consecutive meetings without leave** vacates office.

**Business:** **Section 5(b) banking** and **Section 6(1)** business, but mainly **loans to small and marginal farmers, labourers, artisans, small entrepreneurs, marketing and service societies and self-help groups** in the notified area.

**Accounts and audit:** closed on **31 March**; auditors approved by the **Central Government**; reports **laid before Parliament**; the **sponsor bank monitors** the RRB through **inspection, internal audit and scrutiny**.

**Amalgamation:** the **Central Government** may amalgamate two or more RRBs by notification, **preserving employees' service**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: RRBs combine local rural focus with ownership split between the Centre, a State and a sponsor bank.

self_check.prompt_text: Who sponsors a Regional Rural Bank and what share of its capital does the sponsor bank hold, as the courseware states?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A sponsor bank, holding 35 per cent of the issued capital.

items.title: Nationalised banks: capital, board and meetings
items.core_explanation_md:
**Source:** the **Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts, 1970 and 1980**; the **undertakings of 20 banks** passed to **corresponding new banks**. Each is a **body corporate** with **perpetual succession** that does **Section 5(b)** banking and **Section 6(1)** business.

**Capital:** under the **2006 Amendment** banks may raise **equity or preference capital** by **public issue, preferential allotment or private placement**, but the **Central Government must hold at least 51 per cent** at all times, and **no other shareholder** may exercise **voting rights above 1 per cent**.

**Control:** the **board** has **superintendence, direction and management**, following **Reserve Bank and Government policies**; the **Central Government** can give **public interest directions** after consulting the **Governor**. **Section 9** lets the Government make **schemes** (**Nationalised Banks (Management and Miscellaneous Provisions) Schemes, 1970 and 1980**) on the **board, chairman and MD, directors' terms, disqualification, meetings, committees and capital**; **Section 19** lets the board make **regulations** with Reserve Bank and Government consent.

**Board composition:** **Chairman and Managing Director** (a separate **Chairman** and **MD and CEO** in larger banks); **up to four other whole-time directors** (raised from three in August 2019); **one Central Government official**; **one regulation or supervision expert** on the **Reserve Bank's recommendation**; **one workmen** and **one officer** director; **one chartered accountant of at least 15 years' experience**; and **up to six other** Government nominees. **Other shareholders** elect **up to three directors**. All must be **fit and proper**.

**Meetings:** **at least six a year and at least one in each quarter**; **15 days' notice**; **quorum one-third** of directors in office; video conferencing allowed.

**Committees:** the **Management Committee** and **Credit Approval Committee** (**Sections 13 and 13A**) and other committees (**Section 14**).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 51 per cent and 1 per cent rules keep control with the Government while allowing public shareholding.

self_check.prompt_text: What minimum share of the equity must the Central Government hold in a nationalised bank?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Fifty-one per cent.

items.title: Banking Regulation Act sections that apply to public sector banks; disinvestment and mergers
items.core_explanation_md:
**Section 51** lists which provisions of the **Banking Regulation Act** apply to **SBI, nationalised banks and RRBs**. The rest do **not** apply because their **own statutes** modify or override them. Applicable sections include:

| Sections | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| **10** | Restrictions on employment |
| **13-15** | Commission and brokerage on shares, unpaid capital, **dividend** |
| **17** | **Reserve fund** |
| **19-21A** | **Subsidiaries**, **Reserve Bank power over advances** |
| **23-28** | **Places of business**, **percentage of assets** |
| **29** (except 3), **29A** | **Accounts** and **associate enterprises** |
| **30(1B), (1C), (2)** | **Special audit** and **auditors** |
| **31** | **Returns** |
| **34** | **Accounting provisions** not retrospective |
| **35, 35A, 35AA, 35AB** | **Inspection**, **directions**, **insolvency resolution and stressed assets** |
| **36** (except 1(d)) | **Reserve Bank powers** |
| **45Y-45ZF** | **Records**, **paid instruments**, **nomination**, **lockers** |
| **46-48** | **Penalties** and **cognisance** |
| **50, 52, 53** | **No compensation claims**, **rules**, **exemptions** |

**Disinvestment:** the **1993 SBI Amendment** made shares **Rs 100 each** and moved the voting cap to **up to 10 per cent**; the **1994 and 1995 amendments** to the **nationalisation Acts** allowed **public shareholding**, a **Rs 1,500 crore** authorised capital (**Rs 10 shares**, adjustable up to **Rs 3,000 crore**), a **1 per cent voting cap** and a **register of shareholders**.

**Mergers:** the courseware records the **August 2019 plan** merging 10 public sector banks into four from **1 April 2020**, with customers treated as customers of the **transferee banks**; the current count and later changes are not taught here.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Section 51 is why the Banking Regulation Act applies to government-owned banks only in part.

self_check.prompt_text: Which section of the Banking Regulation Act lists the provisions that apply to SBI, nationalised banks and RRBs?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Section 51.

items.title: Co-operative banks: applicability, definitions and loan restrictions
items.core_explanation_md:
**Which law:** a bank in **one State** follows the **State Co-operative Societies Act**; a bank in **several States** follows the **Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act**. These govern **constitution**; **banking business** is regulated by the **Banking Regulation Act** as modified by **Part V (Section 56)**, applied by the **1965 Act**.

**Definitions (Section 5(cci)):** a **co-operative bank** is a **State co-operative bank**, a **central co-operative bank** or a **primary co-operative bank**. A **primary co-operative bank** is a society **other than a primary agricultural credit society** that: (i) has **banking as its primary object or principal business**; (ii) has **paid-up share capital and reserves of not less than Rs 1 lakh**; (iii) has **bye-laws that do not admit another co-operative society as a member** (except by subscribing from State Government funds). A **State co-operative bank** is the **principal society in a State** financing other societies; a **central co-operative bank** is the **principal society in a district**.

**Name:** only co-operative banks may use **bank, banker or banking** (a co-operative bank must use at least one); **exempt** are **primary credit societies**, societies protecting the **mutual interest of co-operative banks or land development banks**, and certain **employees' societies**.

**Capital:** **at least Rs 1 lakh** of paid-up capital and reserves; a **primary credit society becoming a primary co-operative bank** gets **two years** (extendable by **one**); **real and exchangeable value** counts; the **Reserve Bank decides** disputes.

**Cash reserve:** other than scheduled banks, **3 per cent** of demand and time liabilities; **scheduled** banks follow **Section 42 of the RBI Act**.

**Section 20 restrictions:** **no loans on own shares**; **no unsecured loans to directors**, to **firms or private companies in which a director is partner, managing agent or guarantor**, to **individuals whom a director guarantees**, or to a **company in which the chairman is managing agent or director**. **Exceptions:** unsecured advances against **bills for supplies to Government** and **bona fide trade bills**. From **1 October 2003** the Reserve Bank **bars all credit to directors and their relatives and related firms**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The primary co-operative bank definition screens out agricultural credit societies and ties the label to a banking business.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the three conditions in the definition of a primary co-operative bank?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Banking is its primary object, paid-up capital and reserves are at least Rs 1 lakh, and its bye-laws do not allow another co-operative society as a member (except through State funds).

items.title: Co-operative banks: licensing, branches, liquid assets, accounts, inspection and deposit insurance
items.core_explanation_md:
**Licence (Section 22):** needed to carry on banking, but **primary credit societies are exempt**. Societies already banking at the 1965 commencement had **one year** and had to **apply within three months**; a **primary credit society that becomes a primary co-operative bank** applies **within three months**; it may continue **until rejection**.

**Branches:** **prior Reserve Bank permission** to open or relocate except **within the same city, town or village**; **temporary branches** (up to **one month**) at exhibitions are free; **central co-operative banks** may open **within their area of operation**; applications go **through NABARD** with an **advance copy to the Reserve Bank** (primary co-operative banks excluded).

**Liquid assets (Section 24):** **not less than 25 per cent** (the Reserve Bank may fix **up to 40 per cent**), held on **any day**; balances with the **State or central co-operative bank** count; a **return** goes to the Reserve Bank (and **NABARD** for banks other than primary).

**Accounts:** balance sheet and profit and loss account **as on the last working day of the year**, in **Third Schedule forms**, **three copies with the auditor's report within six months** to the Reserve Bank (and **NABARD** for State and central co-operative banks).

**Inspection (Section 35):** applies with **minor modifications**; **officers of the State co-operative bank** may inspect a **primary co-operative bank**; reports may go to the **State bank or the Registrar**.

**Deposit insurance:** under **Section 13C** the bank **must be registered with the DICGC**; registration may be **cancelled** if the bank is **barred from deposits**, loses its **licence**, is **wound up**, stops being **eligible**, **converts to a non-banking society**, is **amalgamated** or **transfers its deposits**. An **eligible co-operative bank** (**Section 2(gg)**) is one whose law requires **Reserve Bank sanction for winding up, compromise, amalgamation or reconstruction** and allows **supersession of the board by an administrator for up to five years in aggregate** at the Reserve Bank's requirement.

**Winding up (Section 13D):** the Reserve Bank may **require winding up** where the bank **fails Section 11**, **loses its licence**, is **barred from deposits**, **keeps contravening** the Act after notice, is **unable to pay debts**, or a **compromise cannot be worked**. It is **deemed unable to pay** if it refuses a **lawful demand** within **two working days** (office, branch or agency of the Reserve Bank at that place) or **five working days** (elsewhere) and the Reserve Bank **certifies**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Reserve Bank, NABARD and the Registrar all have a role, which is why the sector faces dual control.

self_check.prompt_text: Through whom does a co-operative bank (other than a primary co-operative bank) route its branch licence application to the Reserve Bank?
self_check.expected_takeaway: NABARD, with an advance copy to the Reserve Bank.

items.title: The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 and co-operative banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Dates:** enacted on **29 September 2020**, deemed in force from **26 June 2020**; Section 4 for **primary co-operative banks** from **29 June 2020**; for **State and central co-operative banks** from a date the Central Government notifies. It replaced the **June 2020 Ordinance** and brought **1,482 urban and 58 multi-State co-operative banks** under **closer Reserve Bank supervision**.

**Main features:**

- The Reserve Bank can start a **scheme of reconstruction or amalgamation** (**Section 45**) including for a co-operative bank.
- During a **moratorium** the bank **cannot grant loans or make investments** (**Section 45(3)**).
- Co-operative banks may issue **equity, preference or special shares** (face value or premium) to **members or residents of their area**, and **unsecured debentures or bonds of 10 years or more**, with **prior Reserve Bank approval** (**Section 12 as applied by Section 56**).
- **No right to demand payment** on **surrender** of shares.
- The Reserve Bank may **exempt** co-operative banks from provisions on **employment, qualification of directors and chairman** (**Section 53A**).
- The Reserve Bank may **supersede the board of a multi-State co-operative bank for up to five years** (**Section 36AAA**).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 2020 changes give the Reserve Bank the same corrective tools for co-operative banks as it has for commercial banks.

self_check.prompt_text: For up to how long may the Reserve Bank supersede the board of a multi-State co-operative bank under Section 36AAA?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Up to five years.

items.title: Private sector banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Private sector banks** are those whose **majority stake is held by private individuals or entities**; mostly **companies under the Companies Act**, governed also by the **Banking Regulation Act** and the **Reserve Bank of India Act**.

**Two groups:** **old private sector banks** (existing **before 1968**) and **new private sector banks** (set up **after the 1990s**). The courseware counts **21** in all as at **31 March 2021** (not taught as current).

The new banks grew because they began with a **clean slate**, used **advanced technology** and served a mostly **affluent clientele** with **error-free, quick and efficient service**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Private banks follow company law as well as banking law, which is why they differ from statutory-corporation banks.

self_check.prompt_text: Under which statute are most private sector banks incorporated?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Companies Act.
