items.title: Differentiated banks: payments banks, small finance banks, HDBS and VDBS
items.core_explanation_md:
**Differentiated banks** work in a **niche** with a **limited range of services**, a **different regulatory dispensation**, or a different **capital requirement, scope or area**. Examples include **urban co-operative banks**, **primary agricultural credit societies**, **regional rural banks**, **local area banks**, **payments banks** and **small finance banks**.

**Nachiket Mor Committee models:**

- **HDBS (Horizontally Differentiated Banking System):** banks **specialise in one or more of payments, deposits and credit**.
- **VDBS (Vertically Differentiated Banking System):** a **full-service bank** differentiated by **size, geography or sector**.

**Advantages:** **specialisation**, **long-term infrastructure lending** by banks with the right risk skills, **small unsecured credit**, closing **MSME financing gaps** (asset and cash-flow lending, leasing, factoring), **customised regulation** and **lower intermediation cost**.

**Payments banks:** serve **migrant workers, low income households, small businesses**; accept **demand deposits**, issue **ATM and debit cards (not credit cards)**, offer **payments and remittances**, act as **business correspondent**, and **distribute simple non-risk sharing products** (mutual funds, insurance); they **cannot lend**; they **invest most deposits in short government securities** and hold the **CRR**. The courseware figures (**Rs 100 crore capital**, **3 per cent leverage**, **40 per cent promoter contribution**) are dated and not taught.

**Small finance banks:** **basic banking** (deposits and loans) to **unserved and underserved** groups: **small business units, small and marginal farmers, micro and small industries**; **no area restriction**; **CRR and SLR** as for other scheduled banks; **priority sector lending of 75 per cent of adjusted net bank credit**, with **half of the loans small** (up to **Rs 25 lakh**) (courseware, dated). The numbers are held back.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Differentiated banks widen access by letting specialists operate under tailored rules instead of full universal-bank rules.

self_check.prompt_text: What does HDBS stand for in the Nachiket Mor Committee proposals?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Horizontally Differentiated Banking System.

items.title: Local Area Banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Purpose (1996 decision):** to **bridge gaps in credit** and provide **cost-effective financial intermediation in rural and semi-urban areas**.

**Norms (courseware):** minimum start-up capital **Rs 5 crore**, brought up-front by the promoters; **NRI** contribution and **family** holding **not above 40 per cent** within three years of licensing; **individual voting rights limited to 10 per cent** (**Section 12(2)**); **area of operation usually up to three geographically contiguous districts**; **registered as a public limited company**, a **partnership firm** or an **LLP**; **licensed under the Banking Regulation Act** and may be on the **Second Schedule**; subject to **Reserve Bank prudential norms**; **priority sector and MSME lending norms** apply. A LAB may open **one branch in an urban centre** in each district at the start, the rest in **rural and semi-urban centres**.

**Role:** to **mobilise rural savings** and invest them **locally** and provide **normal universal banking services**.

**Present position (courseware):** of about **227 applications**, **10 licences** were approved; **two** LABs were operating as at **January 2022**. Their relevance has **declined** with **small finance banks**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: LABs were meant to tie local deposits to local credit, but few survived.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the usual maximum number of geographically contiguous districts in a Local Area Bank area of operation?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Three districts.

items.title: What an NBFC is and who regulates it
items.core_explanation_md:
A **Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC)** is a **company registered under the Companies Act** whose business is **loans and advances**, **acquiring shares, stocks, bonds, debentures or similar securities**, **leasing**, **hire-purchase**, **insurance** or **chit business**. It does **not** include an institution whose **principal business** is **agriculture, industry, buying or selling goods (other than securities)**, **services** or **buying, selling or constructing immovable property**.

**Regulator:** the **Department of Non-Banking Supervision** of the **Reserve Bank**, under **Chapters III B, III C and V** of the **RBI Act, 1934**.

**Three aims:** **depositor protection**, **consumer protection** and **financial stability**.

**Tools:** **cancel the certificate of registration**, **prohibit deposit-taking**, **file criminal cases** and, in extreme cases, **petition for winding up**.

**Scale based regulation:** because many NBFCs became **systemically significant**, the Reserve Bank issued the **revised scale based framework** on **22 October 2021**, effective **1 October 2022**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: An NBFC lends like a bank but does not accept cheque-withdrawable deposits and is not regulated as a bank.

self_check.prompt_text: Which Reserve Bank department regulates NBFCs?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Department of Non-Banking Supervision.

items.title: NBFCs and inclusive growth
items.core_explanation_md:
NBFCs reach customers that banks serve poorly: **small ticket personal loans**, **two and three wheeler finance**, **trucks and used commercial vehicles**, **farm equipment** and **working capital** for **MSMEs**, with **simpler procedures** and **flexible repayment**, though at **higher cost**.

| Segment | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **MSMEs** | Credit for an **employment-rich sector** that often **lacks formal credit** |
| **NBFC-MFIs** | **Loans, savings, money transfer and micro insurance** for poor people |
| **Gold loan NBFCs** | **Loans against gold jewellery** with **quick, simple sanction** |
| **Second hand vehicles** | **Finance for road transport operators**, an area few others serve |
| **Affordable housing** | **Small ticket home loans** with **relaxed documentation** for low income buyers |

**Economic benefits:** **mobilising resources**, **capital formation**, **long-term and specialised credit**, **employment**, **developing financial markets**, **attracting foreign grants** and helping to **break the poverty cycle**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: NBFCs fill gaps in rural, small-ticket and unorganised-sector credit that mainstream banks find costly to serve.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two segments in which NBFCs promote inclusive growth.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example MSME credit and gold loans (or micro finance, second hand vehicles, affordable housing).

items.title: Registration of NBFCs (Section 45-IA)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Rule:** every NBFC must be **registered with the Reserve Bank** under **Section 45-IA** to **start or carry on** the business. It needs a **certificate of registration** and a **net owned fund (NOF)** of **Rs 25 lakh** or another amount **not exceeding Rs 100 crore** notified by the Reserve Bank (different amounts for different categories); the Reserve Bank has specified **Rs 2 crore** for NBFCs generally, unless a specific requirement is set.

**Exempt from Reserve Bank registration (regulated by others):** **venture capital funds, merchant bankers and stock brokers registered with SEBI**; **insurance companies** registered with **IRDAI**; **Nidhi companies**; **chit fund companies**; **housing finance companies** regulated by the **National Housing Bank**; **stock exchanges** and **mutual benefit companies**.

**Categories (2016 Master Direction):** **systemically important non-deposit taking**, **deposit taking**, **factors** (**Factoring Regulation Act, 2011**), **infrastructure debt fund**, **micro finance institutions** and **infrastructure finance companies**, each with its own **conditions on size, NOF and rating**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Registration lets the Reserve Bank screen entrants; exemptions avoid regulating the same business twice.

self_check.prompt_text: Under which section of the RBI Act must an NBFC register?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Section 45-IA.

items.title: The four layers of scale based regulation
items.core_explanation_md:
| Layer | Who is in it |
| --- | --- |
| **Base Layer** | **Non-deposit taking NBFCs below Rs 1,000 crore** assets; **peer to peer platforms**; **account aggregators**; **non-operative financial holding companies**; NBFCs **not using public funds and with no customer interface** |
| **Middle Layer** | **All deposit taking NBFCs**; **non-deposit taking NBFCs with assets of Rs 1,000 crore and above**; **standalone primary dealers**; **infrastructure debt fund NBFCs**; **core investment companies**; **housing finance companies**; **infrastructure finance companies** |
| **Upper Layer** | NBFCs the **Reserve Bank identifies** by **scoring**; the **top ten by asset size** are always here |
| **Top Layer** | **Ideally empty**; used only if the Reserve Bank finds a **substantial rise in systemic risk** in an Upper Layer NBFC |

**Public funds** include **public deposits, inter-corporate deposits, bank finance and other outside borrowings and debentures**, but **not** instruments **compulsorily convertible into equity within five years**. **Customer interface** means **dealing directly with customers**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Rules become stricter as NBFCs grow more important to the financial system.

self_check.prompt_text: Which NBFCs are always placed in the Upper Layer, according to the courseware?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The top ten eligible NBFCs by asset size.

items.title: Net owned fund, provisioning and NPA recognition
items.core_explanation_md:
**NOF** differs by **category**: examples in the courseware are **Rs 2 crore** for **peer to peer and account aggregators**, **Rs 300 crore** for **infrastructure debt funds** and **infrastructure finance companies**, **Rs 20 crore** for **housing finance companies**, **Rs 100 crore** for **mortgage guarantee companies**, with **higher requirements by 31 March 2025 and 2027** for some categories. The figures are dated and are **not taught** as current.

**Standard asset provisioning for NBFC-UL (from 1 October 2022, as the courseware states):**

| Category | Rate |
| --- | --- |
| **Individual housing loans and loans to small and micro enterprises** | **0.25 per cent** |
| **Housing loans at teaser rates** | **2.00 per cent**, falling to **0.40 per cent** after a year at reset rates |
| **Commercial real estate (residential housing)** | **0.75 per cent** |
| **Other commercial real estate** | **1.00 per cent** |
| **All other loans, including to medium enterprises** | **0.40 per cent** |

**NPA recognition:** **overdue for more than 90 days** for **all NBFCs**, with a **glide path** for Base Layer NBFCs not yet at 90 days: **150 days by 31 March 2024**, **120 days by 31 March 2025**, **90 days by 31 March 2026**.

**Board:** at least **one director** with **bank or NBFC experience**. **IPO funding:** ceiling of **Rs 1 crore per borrower**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Moving to the 90 day rule aligns NBFC asset classification with banks.

self_check.prompt_text: After how many days overdue is an NBFC loan recognised as non-performing under the revised norm?
self_check.expected_takeaway: More than 90 days.

items.title: Capital and prudential guidelines
items.core_explanation_md:
**ICAAP (for NBFC-ML and NBFC-UL):** a **Board-policy-driven internal assessment** of capital needs against **credit, market, operational and other residual risks**, proportionate to **scale and complexity**, on **Pillar 2** lines but not insisted on in the same sense.

**For NBFC-UL:** **Common Equity Tier 1 of at least 9 per cent of risk weighted assets**, a **leverage requirement**, and **differential provisioning** for standard assets.

**Minimum capital ratio (applicable NBFCs):** **Tier I and Tier II not less than 15 per cent** of **risk weighted assets (on and off balance sheet)**; **Tier I at least 10 per cent** (other than **NBFC-MFI** and **IDF-NBFC**); **gold-lending NBFCs** (**50 per cent or more** of financial assets in gold loans) **Tier I of 12 per cent**.

**Concentration:** a **single exposure limit** (lending plus investment) of **25 per cent of Tier I capital** for a **single borrower** and **40 per cent** for a **single group**, replacing separate limits of **15 + 15 (total 25)** and **25 + 25 (total 40)** percent of owned fund. Extra room: **5 and 10 per cent** more for **infrastructure** exposure; **infrastructure finance companies** may go above by **10 and 15 per cent of owned fund**.

**Other limits:** **sensitive sector exposure** (**capital market and commercial real estate**) under **Board-approved internal limits**, with a **sub-limit for land acquisition**; **restrictions on loans to directors, relatives and senior officers**; **Large Exposure Framework** for the **Upper Layer**; internal limits for **other key sectors** and the **NBFC sector** for NBFC-UL.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Basing limits on Tier I capital ties exposure directly to loss-absorbing capital.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the minimum capital ratio (Tier I plus Tier II) for an applicable NBFC under the courseware?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Fifteen per cent of risk weighted assets.

items.core_explanation_md:
- **Risk Management Committee** (Board or executive level) for overall risks including **liquidity**.
- **Expanded disclosures:** **types of exposure**, **related party transactions**, **loans to directors and senior officers**, **customer complaints**; in annual statements from **31 March 2023**: **corporate governance report**, **auditors' modified opinion**, **exceptional items**, **covenant breaches**, **divergence in asset classification and provisioning** above a threshold.
- **Loans to directors, senior officers and relatives:** **Board-approved policy** (NBFC-BL); stricter rules for ML and UL.
- **Key Managerial Personnel** may not hold office in **any other NBFC-ML or NBFC-UL** (except a **subsidiary**), but may be directors of **NBFC-BLs**.
- **Independent directors:** not on the board of **more than three** NBFC-ML or NBFC-UL at once.
- **Chief Compliance Officer:** **sufficiently senior**, with a **Board-approved role policy**.
- **Compensation policy:** **Remuneration Committee** and principles for **fixed and variable pay**.
- **Other:** committee roles and review calendar, **whistle blower mechanism**, **governance of subsidiaries**, **Core Banking Solution** for NBFCs with **10 or more branches** (**three year** glide path from 1 October 2022).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Governance rules follow the principle that bigger NBFCs get more structure.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Ten or more branches.

items.title: Bank finance to NBFCs and the co-lending model
items.core_explanation_md:
**Bank finance** to registered NBFCs is largely **deregulated**: the **ceiling linked to NOF has been withdrawn** for NBFCs in **asset financing, loan, factoring and investment**; banks may give **working capital and term loans** and finance **second hand assets** under **Board policy**. For **Residuary Non-Banking Companies** bank finance is **limited to NOF**.

**NBFCs not needing registration:** **insurance companies**, **Nidhi companies**, **chit funds**, **stock brokers and merchant bankers** registered with **SEBI**, **housing finance companies** regulated by the **NHB**.

**Not eligible for bank credit (courseware):** **bills discounted by NBFCs** (except **commercial vehicle and two or three wheeler bills** on strict conditions); **NBFC investments in shares and debentures** (stock brokers may get need-based credit on stock in trade); **unsecured loans and inter-corporate deposits**; **loans to their own subsidiaries and group companies**; **finance for IPO subscription** and **secondary market share purchases**.

**Co-lending model:** a **Board-approved policy** and a **Master Agreement** covering **partner selection, products, terms, responsibilities and customer protection**; the bank either **commits irrevocably** to take its share or **retains discretion** to reject loans after **due diligence**; **KYC and outsourcing rules** apply (no unsupervised reliance on third party due diligence); when the bank has discretion it is **like direct assignment**; **no co-lending with an NBFC of the bank's own promoter group**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Banks fund NBFCs but stay out of activities that could move risky speculation into the banking system.

self_check.prompt_text: May a bank enter a co-lending arrangement with an NBFC belonging to its own promoter group?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No.

items.title: Why reforms were needed and the first Narasimham Committee (1991)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Problems before reform:** **many regulators with separate mandates**, **fragmented laws**, **overlapping jurisdictions** and **regulatory arbitrage**; a banking sector marked by **financial repression**: heavy **regulation**, **administered interest rates**, **directed credit**, a **weak structure** and **poor risk management**.

**Narasimham Committee I (Committee on the Financial System, CFS):** set up in **August 1991**, report in **November 1991**; the **first systematic attempt** at reforming the financial system.

- **High SLR and CRR:** together about **53.5 per cent** at the time; the Committee called this a **'tax on the banking system'** and recommended **lowering** it.
- **Directed credit:** priority sector lending without **appraisal, collateral or follow-up** hurt **loan quality**.
- **Interest subsidy:** **timely credit** matters more than **subsidised interest**; subsidies cost banks profit.
- **Other findings:** **too many unviable branches**, **over-stretched command and control** (weak inspection, **unreconciled inter-branch entries**, **frauds**), **poor staff quality**, and **high cost** of small agricultural and small industry loans.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 1991 report set the direction for later bank reforms: lower reserve requirements, less direction and more commercial discipline.

self_check.prompt_text: In which year did the Narasimham Committee on the Financial System report?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 1991 (November 1991).

items.title: Narasimham Committee II and the FSLRC
items.core_explanation_md:
**Narasimham Committee II (Committee on Banking Sector Reforms):** set up in **December 1997**, report in **April 1998**, to review the progress of the **CFS** recommendations. Main ideas:

- **Stronger capital:** **risk weights**, **higher weights where needed**, **higher CRAR**.
- **Asset quality:** **stringent norms**; **Government-guaranteed sticky advances** treated as **NPA**; **interest subsidy for priority sector** to be eliminated or restructured; **asset reconstruction companies**; **strict IRAC (income recognition, asset classification) norms** and **disclosure**.

**Piecemeal reforms 1998-2011:** adopting **Basel norms**, the **SARFAESI Act, 2002** and others.

**FSLRC (Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission):** set up by the **Ministry of Finance** in **March 2011** under **Justice B.N. Srikrishna** after the **2008 Global Financial Crisis**; report in **March 2013**. It aimed to **review, simplify and rewrite the legal and institutional structures** and covered **banking policy, institutional structure, supervisory system and legislative and technological changes**.

**Reform themes:** end **financial repression**; an **efficient, productive and profitable** sector; **market price discovery** and **market determined interest rates**; **operational autonomy**; **competition**; **calibrated opening to the external sector**; **financial stability**. Reforms were grouped by **banking, monetary policy, financial markets and forex**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Narasimham II moved from liberalisation to strengthening the system, and the FSLRC aimed at redesigning financial laws.

self_check.prompt_text: Who headed the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Justice B.N. Srikrishna.

items.title: Banking sector reforms: competition and market forces
items.core_explanation_md:
**Aim:** a **diversified, efficient and competitive** system that improves **allocative efficiency**. **Six groups of reform:** **competition enhancing**, **market forces**, **prudential**, **institutional and legal**, **supervisory** and **technology**.

**Competition enhancing measures:**

- **Operational autonomy** for public sector banks and **raising equity** from the market (**up to 49 per cent of paid-up capital**, as the courseware says).
- **Transparent entry norms** for **private, foreign and joint venture banks and insurers**; **FDI and portfolio investment**.
- **Foreign banks** via **branches**, **wholly owned subsidiary** or a **subsidiary with up to 74 per cent foreign investment** (courseware).
- **New private banks** after **1991** (**HDFC, ICICI, UTI Bank, IDBI**), **differentiated and small finance banks**, **NBFCs**, **core banking migration** and **VRS (2001)**. By **2008** NPAs had fallen from **about 12 per cent** to **just over 2 per cent**.

**Measures enhancing market forces:** **sharp cuts in pre-emption through reserve requirements**; **market-determined pricing of government securities**; **disbanding of administered interest rates**; a **pure inter-bank call money market**; **auction based repos and reverse repos**; **dematerialisation** and **securitisation markets**; and **Targeted Long Term Repo Operations** (banks borrow **on tap** at the **repo rate** for **up to 3 years** for specific sectors).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Competition and market pricing replaced administered rates and captive government borrowing.

items.title: Prudential, institutional, supervisory and technology reforms
items.core_explanation_md:
**Prudential:** phased adoption of **international best practice** on **capital adequacy**, **income recognition**, **classification and provisioning**; **SLR cut from 38.5 per cent (1991-92) to about 28 per cent in five years**; **CRR cut from 14 per cent to 10 per cent by 1997**; **CRAR introduced in 1992**; later **countercyclical buffer, leverage ratio, LCR, NSFR and large exposure norms (April 2019)**; **KYC and AML**, **Basel II and III**, a **market risk capital charge**, **graded NPA provisioning**, **ownership and governance rules**, **securitisation and debt restructuring**; **deregulated interest rates** and **premature withdrawal** conditions.

**Institutional and legal:** **Lok Adalats**, **debt recovery tribunals**, **asset reconstruction companies**, **SARFAESI Act 2002**, **CIBIL**, **CCIL** (central counterparty for fixed income and money market trades), the **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016**.

**Supervisory:** **Board for Financial Supervision** as apex body; **CAMELS rating**; **risk based supervision**; **consolidated supervision of conglomerates**; **off-site surveillance**; stronger **statutory audit and internal control**; **corporate governance and fit and proper tests**; the **EASE** programme (January 2018) for public sector banks.

**Technology:** **INFINET**, the **Negotiated Dealing System**, the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007**, **RTGS, NEFT, ECS, ATMs, mobile and internet banking, IMPS and UPI**, plus **AI, machine learning, robotics, fintech tie-ups and blockchain**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Reserve requirements fell sharply, replaced by capital based discipline and market tools.

self_check.prompt_text: To what level did the CRR fall from 14 per cent by 1997 as per the courseware?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Ten per cent.

items.title: Reforms in monetary policy and in the money, government securities and capital markets
items.core_explanation_md:
**Monetary policy aims:** **price stability** and **adequate credit for productive sectors** to support growth. **Changes:** **broad money** was dropped as the intermediate target for a **multiple indicator approach**; **direct instruments** (**administered rates, reserve requirements, selective credit control**) gave way to **indirect instruments** (**open market operations**).

**Liquidity tools:**

- **Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF):** **repo and reverse repo auctions** form a **corridor** for the overnight rate and signal policy.
- **Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), 8 April 2022:** the **floor** of the policy corridor; the **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)** is the **ceiling**.
- **Open market operations:** manage liquidity from **capital flows**.
- **Market Stabilization Scheme (MSS):** absorbs **enduring capital inflows** without disturbing LAF.

**Money market:** **interest rate deregulation** from the late **1980s**, **Commercial Paper and Certificates of Deposit**, **screen based trading**, **rupee swaps and forward rate agreements**, a wider **repo market**, and **tri-party repo** (**10 August 2017**, replacing **CBLO**).

**Government securities:** the **captive SLR market** gave way to **auctions**; **automatic monetisation** through **Ways and Means Advances** ended; since **April 2006** the Reserve Bank does **not** take part in the **primary market**.

**Capital market:** from the **Controller of Capital Issues** to **free pricing and book building**, **corporatised exchanges**, **screen trading**, **futures and options**, **rolling settlement replacing the 14-day cycle and Badla**, and **depositories**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A policy corridor with a floor (SDF) and ceiling (MSF) keeps the overnight rate within a band.

self_check.prompt_text: Which facility forms the floor of the Reserve Bank policy corridor?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF).

items.title: Reforms in the forex market
items.core_explanation_md:
**Before reform:** the market was **virtually non-existent**; exchange earners had to **surrender and buy foreign exchange from the Reserve Bank** at the **reference rate** and trades were **squared by day end**.

**Reform measures:** a **managed floating exchange rate**; a rationalised market structure; **new products** (**options, swaps**); a gradual shift to **capital account convertibility** with **Reserve Bank intervention** as needed.

**Liberalisation:** authorised dealers may **take trading positions** and **borrow and invest overseas** (with Board ratification); banks may set **interest rates on non-resident deposits** and use **derivatives for asset-liability management** within **open position and gap limits**; **exporters, Indians investing abroad and FIIs** may take **forward cover and swaps** against a **genuine underlying**; **FIIs and NRIs** may trade **exchange traded derivatives**; exporters may keep **foreign currency accounts (EEFC)**.

**Result:** a **market-based exchange rate**, **current account convertibility**, relaxed **capital account**, ability to **hold open positions** and **retain foreign exchange**, and **hedging tools**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Forex reforms moved the market from surrender-and-sell control to a market in which participants hedge and trade.

self_check.prompt_text: What does EEFC stand for in forex market reforms?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Exchange Earners Foreign Currency (account).

items.title: The Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Set up:** **December 2010** by the **Government of India**; **chaired by the Finance Minister**; **not a statutory body**.

**Purpose:** to **strengthen and institutionalise** the mechanism for **financial stability**, **financial sector development** and **inter-regulatory coordination**, avoiding **overlap** among **RBI, SEBI, IRDA and PFRDA**.

**Members:** **heads of RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA**; the **Finance Secretary**; **Secretaries of DEA, DFS, Revenue and MeitY**; the **IBBI Chairman**; and the **Chief Economic Adviser**.

**Functions:** **financial stability and development**; **macro-prudential supervision** including **large financial conglomerates**; **inter-regulatory coordination**; **financial literacy and inclusion**.

| Wing | Set up | Head |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **FSDC Sub-Committee** | — | **Governor, RBI** |
| **Inter-regulatory Technical Group (IR-TG)** | **September 2011** | **Executive Director in charge of Financial Stability, RBI** |
| **Technical Group on Financial Inclusion and Financial Literacy (TGFIFL)** | **November 2011** | **Deputy Governor, RBI (financial stability)** |
| **Inter Regulatory Forum for Financial Conglomerates (IRF-FC)** | **August 2012** | **Deputy Governor, RBI (banking supervision)** |
| **Working Group on resolution regime** | **January 2013** (High Level Working Group) | Deputy Governor RBI and Secretary DEA |
| **Macro Financial Monitoring Group (MFMG)** | **16 May 2012** | **Chief Economic Adviser** |
| **Early Warning Group** | **June 2012** | **Deputy Governor, RBI (financial markets)** |

**Crisis Prevention and Monitoring Framework (CPMF)** helps regulators **identify and mitigate emerging threats** and stresses **prevention**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The FSDC is a coordination forum, not a regulator, and relies on its wings for technical work.

items.title: Build an instrument timeline before opening the statute
items.core_explanation_md:
For an instrument problem, separate creation and parties, transfer or negotiation, presentment, dishonour and the particular remedy. Then consult the relevant provision in the version applicable to the facts. A bank collection-protection question is different from a drawer-prosecution question even when both concern the same cheque.

Use the appendix as a route into the full text, not as proof that the heading contains every condition. Record dates, holder status, crossing, payment or collection role, and the alleged defect. Presumptions and statutory protections need their own conditions; dishonour does not establish every civil and criminal consequence at once.

self_check.prompt_text: Why separate collection protection from drawer prosecution?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They concern different actors, conditions and remedies.

items.title: Name the relationship and the event
items.core_explanation_md:
A guarantee problem can involve creditor against surety, surety against principal debtor, or contribution between co-sureties. Start by identifying which relationship is in dispute. Then locate the relevant liability, continuing-guarantee, discharge, security or recourse provision. The fact one surety pays does not make every later claim the same cause of action.

A variation, release, forbearance, revocation or impairment of security can engage different rules. Keep the agreement, consent, transaction dates and amounts available while reading the full text. The appendix section route is a memory aid; the substantive contract unit supplies the independently authored explanation and application work.

items.title: Identify the system event and the responsible participant

items.title: Purpose of the Act, the Rules and the Director powers (Section 13)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Purpose:** the **Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002** was enacted to **prevent money laundering** and to provide for **confiscation of property** derived from or involved in it. Because **banks have been used by launderers**, **Chapter IV** puts **obligations on banking companies, financial institutions and intermediaries**.

**Rules:** the Central Government framed the **Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records...) Rules, 2004** in consultation with the **Reserve Bank**.

**Amendments:** the **2012 Amendment Act** (effective **15 February 2013**) **widened the definition** of money laundering to include **concealment, acquisition, possession and use** of proceeds of crime; the Act was amended again in **2019**.

**Director's powers (Section 13(2)):** if the **Director** finds a **reporting entity, its designated director or employees** failed to comply, the Director may: (a) give a **written warning**; (b) **direct compliance** with specific instructions; (c) direct **periodic reports** on the measures being taken; or (d) **levy a fine** of **not less than Rs 10,000 and up to Rs 1 lakh for each failure**.

**Money Transfer Service Scheme agents** may nominate a **Designated Director** to ensure compliance.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Act places direct duties on banks and gives the Director graded powers short of prosecution.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the range of the fine the Director may levy for each failure under Section 13(2) as the courseware states?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Not less than Rs 10,000 and up to Rs 1 lakh.

items.title: The offence of money laundering (Section 3) and punishment (Section 4)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Section 3:** whoever **directly or indirectly attempts to indulge** or **knowingly assists** or is **knowingly a party** to, or is **actually involved** in, any **process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime**, including its **concealment, possession, acquisition or use**, and **projecting or claiming it as untainted property**, is **guilty of the offence of money laundering**.

**Six activities named:** **concealment**, **possession**, **acquisition**, **use**, **projecting as untainted property** and **claiming as untainted property**.

**A continuing offence:** the process continues **as long as the person is directly or indirectly enjoying the proceeds** in any of these ways.

**Punishment (Section 4):** **rigorous imprisonment of at least three years, up to seven years, and fine**; where the proceeds relate to an offence under **paragraph 2 of Part A of the Schedule**, the maximum becomes **ten years**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The continuing-offence rule means the offence is not complete when the money is first hidden.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the minimum term of imprisonment for the offence of money laundering under Section 4?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Three years of rigorous imprisonment.

items.title: Obligations of reporting entities (Sections 12 to 15) and enhanced due diligence (Section 12AA)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Section 12(1):** every **reporting entity** must: (a) **maintain a record of all transactions** so that **individual transactions can be reconstructed**; (b) **furnish the Director** information on transactions, **attempted or executed**, as prescribed; (c) **maintain identity records** of **clients and beneficial owners**, **account files** and **business correspondence**.

**Section 12(2):** the information is **kept confidential** unless the law provides otherwise.

**Section 12(3):** **transaction records** are kept for **five years from the date of the transaction**.

**Section 12(4):** **identity records** are kept for **five years after the business relationship ends or the account is closed, whichever is later**.

**Section 12(5):** the Central Government may **exempt** a reporting entity or class by notification.

**Enhanced due diligence (Section 12AA, added in 2019):** before each **specified transaction** the entity must **verify the client's identity by Aadhaar authentication**, examine **ownership, financial position and sources of funds**, and **record the purpose and intended nature of the relationship**; if the conditions are **not met**, the transaction **must not be carried out**; suspicious clients are **monitored more closely**; records are kept **five years**. A **specified transaction** includes **cash withdrawals or deposits above a set amount**, **foreign exchange transactions above a set amount**, **high value imports or remittances** and others the Government prescribes.

**Section 14:** **no civil or criminal proceedings** lie against a reporting entity, its directors or officers **for furnishing information to the Director**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Safe harbour for reporting encourages banks to report suspicious activity without fear of liability.

self_check.prompt_text: For how long must identity records of clients be kept after the business relationship ends or the account is closed under Section 12(4)?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Five years, whichever is later.

items.title: PML Rules: records to be maintained (Rule 3), their contents and procedure
items.core_explanation_md:
**Rule 3 (as amended from 27 August 2013)** requires records of:

| Clause | Transaction |
| --- | --- |
| **(A)** | **All cash transactions of more than Rs 10 lakh** (or equivalent in foreign currency) |
| **(B)** | **Series of connected cash transactions each below Rs 10 lakh** within **a month** whose **monthly total exceeds Rs 10 lakh** |
| **(BA)** | **Receipts by non-profit organisations above Rs 10 lakh** |
| **(C)** | **Cash transactions with forged or counterfeit notes**, or forged securities or documents facilitating the transaction |
| **(D)** | **All suspicious transactions**, cash or otherwise (deposits, withdrawals, transfers, loans, investments, contingent liabilities, guarantees, derivatives and collections) |
| **(E)** | **Cross border wire transfers of more than Rs 5 lakh** where either end is in India |
| **(F)** | **Purchase or sale of immovable property valued at Rs 50 lakh or more** that is **registered by the reporting entity** |

**Contents (Rule 4):** the **nature** of the transaction, the **amount and currency**, the **date**, and the **parties**.

**Form (Rule 6):** kept in **hard and soft copies** as the **Reserve Bank or SEBI** specifies.

**Furnishing to the Director (Rule 8):** the **Principal Officer** sends information on **(A), (B), (BA), (C) and (E)** **monthly by the 15th of the next month**; **suspicious transactions (D)** **promptly, within seven working days** of being satisfied that the transaction is suspicious; **(F)** **quarterly by the 15th of the month after the quarter**. **Each day of delay** or of delay in rectifying a mis-reported transaction is **a separate violation**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The thresholds and deadlines are the working reporting calendar of a bank compliance team.

self_check.prompt_text: By which day of the succeeding month must a Principal Officer report monthly cash transactions to the Director under Rule 8?
self_check.expected_takeaway: By the 15th day.

items.title: Verification of the identity of clients and records of identity
items.core_explanation_md:
**At account opening or transaction:** the bank must **verify and keep** the **identity**, **current and permanent address**, **nature of business** and **financial status** of the client. If it cannot do so at once it verifies **within a reasonable time** after the account is opened or the transaction is executed.

| Client | Documents |
| --- | --- |
| **Individual** | A **certified copy of an officially valid document** showing **permanent address**, current address and, where relevant, **nature of business and financial status** |
| **Company** | **Certificate of incorporation**, **memorandum and articles**, **board resolution or power of attorney**, and an **officially valid document of the person operating the account** |
| **Partnership firm** | **Registration certificate**, **partnership deed**, and an **officially valid document of the person acting** |
| **Trust** | **Registration certificate**, **trust deed**, and an **officially valid document of the person acting** |
| **Unincorporated association** | **Managing body resolution**, **power of attorney** and **information on the association's legal existence** |

**Retention:** records on client identity are kept **five years from the date the transactions with the client cease**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Different entities prove their existence and authority with different papers, but all rely on an officially valid document for the person acting.

self_check.prompt_text: Which document is required for a partnership firm in addition to the registration certificate and the officially valid document of the person acting?

items.title: Start with the obligation, then identify the instrument
items.core_explanation_md:
When checking a payment document, ask who undertakes to pay. A **promissory note** records the maker's own unconditional payment undertaking. A **bill of exchange** directs another identified person to pay. Both require writing, the relevant signature, a certain money sum and an identifiable recipient. A document that only records an unpaid balance does not establish the payment undertaking required for a note.

A **cheque** belongs to the bill family, with two extra defining features: the drawee is a specified banker and payment is on demand. Classifying every bank-related document as a cheque would miss these conditions.

self_check.prompt_text: What separates the obligation in a note from the obligation in a bill?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A note is the maker's undertaking; a bill directs another person to pay.

items.title: Electronic form and truncation describe different routes
items.core_explanation_md:
A cheque created electronically under the statutory signature requirements is different from an image made from an existing paper cheque. **Truncation** starts with the paper cheque: an electronic image replaces its further physical movement during clearing.

For a branch reviewer, the first task is to identify which route produced the record. A scanned document is not automatically an electronically drawn cheque. Nor does digitisation remove the need to check the underlying instrument and the duties attached to its processing.

self_check.prompt_text: Does imaging an existing paper cheque make it an electronically drawn cheque?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. It produces the image of a truncated paper cheque; electronic drawing is a separate statutory category.

items.title: Read the transfer instruction before handling delivery
items.core_explanation_md:
A named recipient and a bearer do not follow identical transfer routes. An instrument payable to a named person can be **order paper** even when it omits the words “or order”, provided its wording does not prohibit transfer. Subject to statutory exceptions, order paper is negotiated by the holder's **indorsement and delivery**. Bearer paper is negotiated by **delivery**.

A bank handling an order instrument should therefore distinguish custody from negotiation. Passing an unsigned order instrument to a courier does not supply the missing indorsement. The courier's possession also does not establish an entitlement to the proceeds.

self_check.prompt_text: For order paper, which two steps are ordinarily needed for negotiation?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Indorsement by the holder and delivery, subject to the statutory qualifications.

items.title: An indorsement can identify the next person or restrict the next use
items.core_explanation_md:
A **blank indorsement** contains the indorser's signature alone. A **full indorsement** adds a direction naming the indorsee. The difference concerns the instruction attached to the signature, rather than the physical space used.

Read any limiting words as well. An indorsement can appoint a collecting agent or exclude further negotiation. An operational review should record both who may receive the instrument and what authority the wording gives that person. Treating every signature on the back as an unrestricted transfer would miss these limits.

self_check.prompt_text: Why should a reviewer read words beside an indorsement rather than check the signature alone?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The words may identify an indorsee, restrict further negotiation or create an agency.

items.title: Map the instruction before mapping liability
items.core_explanation_md:
Use a three-part reading of a bill: **who gives the order, who must act on it, and who should receive the money**. These roles are drawer, drawee and payee respectively. They describe functions; the document must still be read to see whether one person occupies more than one role.

The drawee becomes an **acceptor** through signed assent followed by delivery of the bill or notice of the signing to the holder or someone acting for the holder. A private mental decision to pay is not the statutory act of acceptance. The maker of a note undertakes payment directly rather than waiting to become a bill's acceptor.

self_check.prompt_text: What additional event is needed beyond the drawee merely signing assent?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Delivery of the bill or notice of the signing to the holder or a person on the holder's behalf.

items.title: Need and honour address different problems
items.core_explanation_md:
A **drawee in case of need** is an additional person identified on the bill or an indorsement to be approached if needed. **Acceptance for honour** instead follows the specified noting or protest circumstances and is made for the honour of the drawer or an indorser.

When a file mentions a substitute payer, ask how the role arose. A name written in advance as an additional recourse is not the same as an intervention after protest. Keeping that distinction prevents a branch from assigning powers or liabilities from a label that does not fit the instrument's history.

self_check.prompt_text: Does naming an additional recourse automatically make that person an acceptor for honour?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. A drawee in case of need and an acceptor for honour arise in different ways.

items.title: A presumption supplies a starting point, not an unchangeable verdict
items.core_explanation_md:
Negotiable-instrument disputes do not begin with every fact unproved. **Section 118** supplies presumptions about matters such as consideration, the stated date, timing of acceptance and transfer, and the sequence of indorsements. These operate until contrary evidence is proved.

For a bank preparing a disputed-instrument file, the useful distinction is between a presumption and a conclusion immune from challenge. Preserve documents and transaction evidence even when a statutory presumption initially assists the bank. Do not convert “presumed” into “cannot be disputed”.

self_check.prompt_text: Why should supporting records be preserved even when Section 118 supplies a presumption?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The presumptions can be rebutted by evidence; they are not conclusive proof.

items.title: Title problems can change who must prove due-course status
items.core_explanation_md:
The presumption that a holder is a holder in due course has a qualification. Where the instrument was obtained through the offence, fraud or unlawful-consideration circumstances specified in **Section 118(g)**, the holder bears the burden of proving that status. This requires examining the acquisition rather than simply pointing to possession.

**Section 119** deals with a different evidential route: once protest is proved in a suit on a dishonoured instrument, dishonour is presumed unless disproved. It does not turn protest into an answer to every disputed issue, such as title or consideration.

self_check.prompt_text: Does proved protest conclusively settle title to an instrument?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. Section 119 concerns a rebuttable presumption of dishonour, not a general determination of title.

items.title: A balance enquiry is only part of the payment decision
items.core_explanation_md:
A cheque-payment decision needs both **funds** and **authority**. Under Section 31, the drawee must have enough of the drawer's money properly available for the cheque and must be duly required to pay it. An apparent credit balance does not answer whether a court restraint, earmarking or other lawful restriction prevents its use.

The operational sequence is to inspect the payment instruction, establish the funds available for that instruction, and resolve any restriction before deciding. Checking only the balance can produce both a wrongful refusal and a payment the bank had no authority to make.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can sufficient gross balance still fail the Section 31 funds test?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The funds must also be properly applicable to that cheque; a lawful restriction can prevent their use.

items.title: Wrongful dishonour concerns the drawer's resulting loss
items.core_explanation_md:
Section 31 links the drawee's default to compensation of the **drawer** for loss or damage caused by it. The relevant investigation records the cheque, the usable funds, the mandate, the reason for refusal and the loss attributed to that refusal.

Do not treat the cheque amount as an automatic fixed compensation award. Nor should the file assume that the named payee is the statutory claimant under this particular section. Other causes of action need their own legal analysis; the immediate task is to apply Section 31 to the correct relationship and consequences.

self_check.prompt_text: Is compensation under Section 31 automatically equal to the cheque amount?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. The section addresses the drawer's loss or damage caused by the default.

items.title: Payment in due course is a combined test
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank should not reduce **payment in due course** to one successful check. Section 10 combines the instrument's apparent terms, good faith, absence of negligence and circumstances that do not reasonably suggest the recipient is not entitled. Possession is relevant, but it is not the entire test.

Consider a payment file with a clean-looking image but an unresolved warning about the presenter's entitlement. The clean image addresses only part of the decision. The bank still needs to deal with the warning; a favourable result on one condition cannot substitute for the others.

self_check.prompt_text: Can good faith alone establish payment in due course?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. Apparent tenor, care and the circumstances of entitlement also matter.

items.title: Investigate warning signs before relying on a payment defence
items.core_explanation_md:
The practical question is what a careful payment decision should have noticed from the instrument and surrounding circumstances. A mismatch with the visible payment date, an unresolved instruction affecting payment or a reasonable concern about entitlement needs attention before release.

This is not a promise that a banker must discover every concealed fraud. The learning task is to distinguish a hidden problem despite ordinary care from a warning that was available and ignored. The available evidence and the checks actually performed belong in the file.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does an ignored entitlement warning matter even where the presenter physically holds the cheque?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Section 10 requires circumstances without reasonable grounds to doubt entitlement; possession alone cannot satisfy that requirement.

items.title: Ask what kind of defect the paying-bank protection addresses
items.core_explanation_md:
Section 85 addresses the paying drawee's discharge in defined cheque situations. For an **order cheque** that purports to carry the payee's indorsement, payment must still be in due course. The provision is therefore not permission to ignore irregularities or reasonable doubts.

The difference between an indorsement and the drawer's mandate is crucial. A defence addressing a purported payee indorsement must not be treated as a general validation of a forged drawer signature. A bank should first identify the instrument and the alleged defect, then test the conditions of the particular protection.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is “all forgeries are covered by Section 85” an unsafe shortcut?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Its conditions concern specified cheque payment and indorsement situations; they do not validate every defect or forged mandate.

items.title: Original bearer wording and inter-office drafts have specific rules
items.core_explanation_md:
For a cheque **originally payable to bearer**, Section 85(2) allows discharge through payment in due course to the bearer despite later full, blank or restrictive indorsements of the kind described there. The word **originally** matters when selecting the provision. This rule does not abolish separate crossing duties.

Section 85A applies to the specified **order-on-demand draft drawn by one office on another office of the same bank**. A document called a “draft” in conversation does not automatically meet that definition. Check the offices, the bank identity, the demand terms and the purported payee indorsement.

self_check.prompt_text: Which bank-identity condition matters under Section 85A?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The draft must be drawn by one office of a bank on another office of the same bank.

items.title: Identify the changed obligation and the party affected
items.core_explanation_md:
A material alteration changes the instrument's legal or commercial effect: changing the amount, the payment timing or the beneficiary can change what a party agreed to. The consequence is not accurately described by saying that every altered document is void against everyone.

Under Section 87, focus on a person who was already a party when the material change was made and did not consent. The section also recognises the original parties' common intention and is subject to specified statutory provisions. A careful file records the original terms, the change, who was a party at that time and what consent or authority is evidenced.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is party timing relevant when an instrument has been materially altered?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Section 87 concerns a non-consenting party already on the instrument when the alteration was made; later acceptance or indorsement has a separate rule.

items.title: Later acceptance and permitted completion need separate treatment
items.core_explanation_md:
Section 88 provides that an **acceptor or indorser is bound despite an earlier alteration**. Compare that with a person whose existing obligation was changed without consent: the sequence of events can lead to different results.

Also avoid classifying every permitted addition as an unauthorised material alteration. Section 87 is expressly subject to provisions including completion of inchoate stamped instruments, conversion of a blank indorsement into a full one, qualified acceptance and crossing. Whether an addition falls within one of those provisions must be established from its facts, rather than guessed from the presence of new handwriting.

self_check.prompt_text: Does Section 87 justify treating every later annotation as invalid?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. Consent, common intention, the statutory qualifications and later-party rules must be considered.

items.title: Hidden alteration does not remove the due-course conditions
items.core_explanation_md:
Section 89 addresses an alteration that does **not appear on presentation**, including the specified crossing situations. Its protection requires payment according to the apparent terms and otherwise in due course. The section does not excuse ignoring an alteration that is visible or other circumstances that defeat the due-course test.

Separate the questions in a disputed payment: what change was made, whether it was apparent at payment, what ordinary checks were performed and whether the rest of the payment met the required conditions. Later forensic discovery of a change does not by itself answer all of them.

self_check.prompt_text: Does discovering an alteration later prove that Section 89 protection was unavailable?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. Apparency at payment and the remaining statutory conditions must be examined.

items.title: Check both links in the cheque-image chain
items.core_explanation_md:
Truncation creates more than one integrity task. Under Section 89(2), the bank or clearing house must ensure the image's apparent terms match the paper cheque when truncating and transmitting it. Under Section 89(3), a receiving bank or clearing house verifies with the transmitting party that the image received is exactly the image sent.

These checks answer different questions. A perfectly transmitted image can still misrepresent the paper cheque. Separately, Section 131 Explanation II requires the collecting banker holding the cheque for truncation to check its apparent genuineness with ordinary care. Passing a transmission check does not replace that original-instrument check.

self_check.prompt_text: Can proof that received and transmitted images match establish that the image matches the paper original?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. Image-to-image transmission integrity and image-to-original exactness are different checks.

items.title: Separate custody, entitlement and due-course acquisition
items.core_explanation_md:
A payment file may name the person carrying an instrument, the person entitled to recover on it and a later acquirer claiming special status. These are not interchangeable descriptions. Under Section 8, **holder** concerns entitlement in one's own name to possession and to receive or recover the amount. Physical custody can belong to an agent while entitlement remains elsewhere.

For **holder in due course**, Section 9 adds acquisition for consideration, the required bearer/order status, acquisition before the amount becomes payable, and no sufficient cause to believe the transferor's title defective. Check the acquisition file rather than inferring all of this from the label “holder”.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does physical custody alone not decide holder-in-due-course status?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Entitlement and the consideration, timing, instrument-status and title conditions must also be established.

items.title: Early credit does not settle the bank's legal capacity
items.core_explanation_md:
A collecting bank may credit a customer before receiving the cheque proceeds. That timing alone does not decide whether the bank acts as collecting agent or takes the instrument in another capacity. **Section 131 Explanation I** expressly allows receipt for a customer within the section despite credit before receipt.

If the bank claims holder-for-value or holder-in-due-course rights, examine the actual transaction and the applicable conditions. Equally, do not deny every collecting-bank defence solely because an advance credit exists. Preserve the capacity analysis separately from the accounting timestamp.

self_check.prompt_text: Does a credit entry before collection automatically remove Section 131 protection?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. Explanation I addresses early credit; the actual capacity and remaining conditions still need analysis.

items.title: Identify the collecting service and its conditions
items.core_explanation_md:
A collecting bank receives payment for its customer; the paying bank honours the drawer's instruction. **Section 131** addresses the collecting side where title proves defective. It requires the specified crossed cheque, collection for a customer, good faith and absence of negligence. It does not declare every collection safe or provide a substitute for the paying bank's separate duties.

A reviewer should record the crossing, the customer relationship, the bank's capacity and the reasonable checks performed. A customer relationship helps establish one condition; it does not excuse ignored inconsistencies or apparent tampering.

self_check.prompt_text: Can collection for an existing customer alone establish Section 131 protection?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. Crossing, good faith and absence of negligence also matter.

items.title: A crossing controls the route; not negotiable controls title
items.core_explanation_md:
A **general crossing** requires payment to a banker. A **special crossing** identifies the banker through whom payment must pass, allowing the specified banker-agent collection route. Section 129 addresses the paying banker's liability for loss caused by payment outside those routes.

Adding **not negotiable** concerns title: a taker cannot obtain or pass a better title than the transferor had. It does not simply mean that no transfer can take place. Section 131A extends this chapter to the particular inter-office drafts defined by Section 85A. Keep routing, title quality and collecting-bank protection as separate questions in a dispute.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a not-negotiable crossing limit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The quality of title a taker can obtain or pass, rather than prohibiting every transfer.

items.title: A return memo is an event in the statutory sequence
items.core_explanation_md:
A cheque returned unpaid does not by itself establish that every condition of Section 138 has been met. The statutory sequence concerns a legally enforceable debt or liability, the specified return grounds, presentment within the applicable period, written demand and the drawer's failure to pay within the required time after receipt of notice.

Keep the clocks separate: Section 138's demand window runs from receipt of bank information, while the payment window runs from receipt of the notice. The statutory text states six months or the cheque's validity, whichever is earlier, for presentment. Do not treat six months as the bank's current operational validity rule; the RBI rule needs its own source check.

Section 139 supplies a rebuttable presumption about receipt for debt or liability, rather than an unchallengeable finding.

self_check.prompt_text: Why should a case file record both receipt of the return information and receipt of the demand notice?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Different statutory time windows use those different trigger events.

items.title: Select the liable party and the complaint route carefully
items.core_explanation_md:
For company cases, Section 141 addresses the company and persons in charge of and responsible for its business at the relevant time, with stated defences and qualifications. It also addresses consent, connivance and neglect by specified officers. A job title alone is an incomplete analysis.

Section 142 specifies a written complaint by the payee or holder in due course, ordinarily within one month of the cause of action, with a sufficient-cause provision for delay. For collection through an account, its jurisdiction rule points to the branch where that account is maintained; otherwise it points to the drawer's drawee-bank branch. Deposit at another branch does not automatically move the account-based venue. Section 147 provides for compounding; it is not automatic acquittal upon dishonour.

self_check.prompt_text: Does deposit through a different branch automatically relocate the account-based jurisdiction under Section 142?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. The statute deems delivery to the branch where the payee or holder in due course maintains the account.

items.title: A shared percentage can conceal a different legal base
items.core_explanation_md:
**Section 143A** concerns interim compensation during trial. In the statutory text, the court may order it at the specified stage, and the amount must not exceed **20% of the cheque amount**. This is a ceiling on the amount of such an order.

**Section 148** concerns a deposit on appeal against conviction. Its stated minimum is **20% of the fine or compensation awarded by the trial court**, and the deposit is additional to interim compensation. This is a floor with a different base.

The text also supplies payment periods, possible court-directed extensions for sufficient cause and repayment provisions after acquittal. These are conditional court processes. Do not describe the two percentages as automatic deductions made by a bank, or infer a mandatory order in every case. Current judicial interpretation and exam-cutoff applicability remain under review.

self_check.prompt_text: Which quantity is the base for each percentage?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Section 143A uses the cheque amount; Section 148 uses the trial-court fine or compensation.

items.title: Compare the two percentage bases before calculating
items.core_explanation_md:
A training file has a cheque amount of **Rs 7,50,000** and a trial-court compensation award of **Rs 9,00,000**. For the arithmetic illustration, assume a Section 143A order at its 20% ceiling and a Section 148 order at its 20% floor.

The first base is the cheque amount: 20% gives **Rs 1,50,000**. The second base is the trial-court award: 20% gives **Rs 1,80,000**. If both stated amounts are payable, the appeal deposit is additional, giving **Rs 3,30,000** in this illustration.

Do not swap the two bases, assume every court makes an order, or present the floor and ceiling as a single fixed tariff. This example teaches arithmetic under the stated statutory-text assumptions; judicial application remains subject to review.

items.title: Find the applicable layer before deciding a forex request
items.core_explanation_md:
**FEMA** supplies the legal framework for foreign exchange; it does not put every transaction limit or processing condition in one place. A bank needs the Act, the applicable rules or regulations, RBI directions and the conditions of its own authorisation to decide a request. Knowing the purpose of the Act is not the same as establishing permission for a particular transaction.

Its purpose includes facilitating external trade and payments and orderly development of the foreign-exchange market. Its reach is also wider than a transaction physically performed at an Indian counter: specified overseas branches, offices and agencies owned or controlled by residents, and contraventions abroad by persons to whom the Act applies, are within Section 1.

For a transaction file, identify the parties, location, instrument, purpose and rule version before concluding that an overseas connection puts it outside FEMA.

self_check.prompt_text: Can the Act's broad trade-facilitation purpose alone authorise a particular remittance?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. The applicable transaction rules, directions and authorisation conditions still need to be checked.

items.title: Do not use foreign cash as a shortcut for foreign exchange
items.core_explanation_md:
**Foreign currency** means currency other than Indian currency. **Foreign exchange** is broader: it includes foreign-currency deposits, credits and balances and the additional instrument categories specified in Section 2. A file can therefore involve foreign exchange without containing any physical foreign notes.

The definition also captures specified instruments drawn abroad but payable in rupees. **Foreign security** has its own denomination test; rupee redemption or rupee interest/dividends do not automatically remove a foreign-currency-denominated security from the definition. Classify the actual asset and payment terms rather than using settlement currency or the presence of cash as the only test.

self_check.prompt_text: Can rupee payment alone prove that an instrument falls outside all FEMA foreign-exchange definitions?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. The definitions include specified rupee-payable instruments drawn abroad, and foreign security may have rupee redemption or returns.

items.title: Classify the economic effect, then check permission
items.core_explanation_md:
For a **capital account transaction**, inspect whether the transaction changes the specified cross-border assets or liabilities, including contingent liabilities. For a **current account transaction**, the Act gives examples such as ordinary foreign-trade/service payments, loan interest, family maintenance and education or medical expenses.

Classification is only the first step. “Current” does not mean that the bank may ignore applicable restrictions, and “capital” does not mean that every such transaction is absolutely prohibited. The bank must identify the permitted route, conditions and documentary requirements after classifying the transaction. Keep the classification note and the permission check separate in the file.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Applicable restrictions, authorised-person requirements and documentation still need to be satisfied.

items.title: Contingent obligations matter; authority also depends on the instrument
items.core_explanation_md:
The capital-account definition expressly includes **contingent liabilities**. A reviewer must therefore look beyond an immediate cash movement or a balance-sheet cash entry. A new cross-border obligation can require analysis even before any payment occurs.

The statutory copy also distinguishes the regulatory roles for capital transactions involving debt instruments and those not involving debt instruments: Section 6 assigns specification/prescription roles to RBI and the Central Government respectively, with consultation. The current instrument classification and operative rules still need verification; do not assume one authority or one old rule governs every capital request.

self_check.prompt_text: Can absence of an immediate cash payment by itself rule out capital-account analysis?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. The definition includes contingent liabilities, so the obligation and statutory conditions must be examined.

items.title: Residence is a statutory classification, not a passport label
items.core_explanation_md:
For an individual, Section 2(v) starts with **more than 182 days in the preceding financial year**, then includes purpose and stay qualifications concerning employment, business/vocation and intention to stay for an uncertain period. Do not stop after counting days or substitute a tax-residence rule.

A bank's evidence should cover the relevant year, the reason for departure or arrival and the circumstances of the intended stay. Nationality may be part of identification, but it does not by itself answer FEMA residence. An Indian citizen leaving for overseas employment cannot be classified solely by having an Indian passport or by an earlier day total.

self_check.prompt_text: Which additional evidence should accompany the day count for an individual?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Purpose and circumstances of departure/arrival and stay, including the statutory employment, business and uncertain-period qualifications.

items.title: An entity and its branches require their own residence analysis
items.core_explanation_md:
Section 2 treats **person** broadly, including companies, firms, HUFs and specified bodies and agencies. Residence also has entity-specific limbs: Indian registration/incorporation, an India branch owned or controlled by a non-resident, and an overseas branch owned or controlled by a resident are expressly addressed.

Do not apply the individual's day count to a company or assume a branch has the same classification as its physical address suggests. Equally, do not extend a branch rule automatically to every separately incorporated subsidiary. First identify the legal form, then apply the matching statutory limb.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is an individual's 182-day calculation not the right starting test for an Indian-incorporated company?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The statute has a separate Indian registration/incorporation limb for persons and body corporates.

items.title: Authorisation gives defined scope, not unrestricted permission
items.core_explanation_md:
An **authorised person** is someone with the relevant Section 10 authorisation, such as an authorised dealer, money changer or other specified person. It is not restricted to a natural person. The authorisation is written and conditional.

A forex file needs two permission checks: whether the transaction itself has a lawful route and whether this provider's authorisation covers the proposed service. A customer declaration cannot enlarge the bank's authorised scope. RBI directions and the terms of authorisation remain relevant even when the customer supplies a commercial explanation.

self_check.prompt_text: Can a customer's instruction expand a provider's authorisation?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. The transaction must fit the provider's authorisation and the applicable legal permissions.

items.title: Record the enquiry and the reason for the decision
items.core_explanation_md:
Section 10(5) requires declarations and information that reasonably satisfy the authorised person about avoiding contravention or evasion. If the customer refuses the requirement or compliance is unsatisfactory, the authorised person must **refuse in writing**. A reason to believe the specified contravention or evasion is contemplated also engages reporting to RBI.

The file should distinguish incomplete evidence from the further reporting condition; do not claim every missing document proves wrongdoing. Sections 11–12 separately support RBI directions, information requests and inspection. The authorisation regime also has specific revocation grounds and safeguards, including the representation opportunity for the non-compliance ground in Section 10(3)(b).

self_check.prompt_text: Why should the written refusal and any reporting decision be separately reasoned?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Unsatisfactory compliance and the statutory reason-to-believe reporting condition are distinct parts of Section 10(5).

items.title: Start with the restriction, then check its statutory qualifications
items.core_explanation_md:
Section 4 restricts resident holding and dealing in the specified foreign exchange, foreign securities and overseas immovable property **except as otherwise provided**. Those opening words matter. For example, Section 6(4) addresses specified assets acquired while the person was non-resident or inherited from a non-resident.

The correct bank workflow is to establish residence, acquisition history and the applicable permission or exception. Neither “all overseas assets are forbidden” nor “anything inherited is unrestricted for every purpose” is a sound substitute. The asset's later use and transaction-specific rules still need analysis.

self_check.prompt_text: Why should an overseas-asset file retain the history of acquisition and prior residence?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Those facts can be relevant to statutory qualifications such as Section 6(4), beyond the general holding restriction.

items.title: Repatriation is a defined outcome with regulated methods
items.core_explanation_md:
Repatriation is not simply a synonym for handing over foreign cash at a counter. Section 2(y) addresses bringing realised foreign exchange into India and the specified sale to an authorised person or notified account holding; it also includes use to discharge a foreign-currency debt or liability. Conditions and applicable permissions must still be checked.

Sections 7–8 separately address export declarations and reasonable steps to realise and repatriate amounts due or accrued, within the period and manner specified by RBI, subject to statutory qualifications. Do not infer one universal deadline from the bare Act or ignore an applicable exemption. The relevant dated RBI direction belongs with the transaction file.

self_check.prompt_text: Does the bare Act supply a single fixed realisation period for every export request?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. It refers to RBI-specified period and manner, with applicable qualifications and exemptions.

items.title: Separate the breach, adjudication and enforcement stages
items.core_explanation_md:
The retrieved Section 13(1) text describes a penalty **upon adjudication**. Its ceiling is up to three times the amount where quantifiable, or up to Rs 2 lakh where not quantifiable. A continuing contravention can attract an additional ceiling of Rs 5,000 for each day **after the first day**. These are ceilings, not automatic fixed charges.

The Act also contains special provisions concerning certain overseas assets and conditional enforcement provisions. Section 14 addresses non-payment and civil-enforcement safeguards; it does not justify the shortcut “every FEMA violation causes immediate arrest”. Identify the particular provision, required authority and procedural conditions before describing the consequence. Current law and operative notifications remain to be verified for release.

self_check.prompt_text: What is wrong with treating a Section 13 ceiling as an automatic debit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A penalty follows adjudication and the statutory ceiling does not itself determine the amount actually imposed.

items.title: A ceiling is not the penalty actually imposed
items.core_explanation_md:
For a training illustration under the retrieved Section 13(1) text, assume a quantifiable contravention involving **Rs 2,40,000** and continuation on **five days after the first day**. The base ceiling is three times the amount: **Rs 7,20,000**. At the stated maximum additional daily amount, five further days add **Rs 25,000**, giving an illustrative combined ceiling of **Rs 7,45,000**.

items.title: Identify the investigating authority and the power invoked

items.title: Equivalent value in India is different from seizure of the foreign asset
items.core_explanation_md:
**Section 37A** addresses suspected foreign assets held contrary to Section 4. The specified Authorised Officer records reasons and may order seizure of **equivalent value situated in India**, subject to the prescribed threshold. The foreign asset and the Indian equivalent-value asset are different objects in this process.

The text requires the seizure order and material to reach the Competent Authority within 30 days and provides for confirmation or setting aside within 180 days, with hearing and court-stay qualifications. Disclosure and bringing the foreign asset back lead to an application and an appropriate order after hearing; seizure does not vanish automatically. An aggrieved person has the specified Tribunal appeal, and the text excludes Section 15 compounding from this section. The threshold amount is not supplied by this batch.

self_check.prompt_text: Does bringing the foreign asset back automatically cancel the Indian seizure order?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. The text provides for an application, hearing and appropriate order, which can include setting aside seizure.

items.title: Read the instruction, the obligation and the service separately
items.core_explanation_md:
A customer's **payment instruction** is an order or authorisation to effect payment. It can generate a **payment obligation** between system participants through clearing or settlement. **Settlement** addresses the payment instructions and can involve funds, securities, foreign exchange or derivatives. Treating these as synonyms makes it hard to see what has actually happened in a payment file.

The **payment system** supplies clearing, payment or settlement services between payer and beneficiary; it need not perform all three services to fit the definition. The definition excludes a stock exchange. A service's commercial name or digital appearance alone does not determine its classification.

self_check.prompt_text: Does receipt of an instruction prove that the resulting obligation has already been settled?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. Instruction, obligation and settlement describe different parts of the process.
